-- - - THE YEAR'S CONSOLATIONS. When January's cold is here, ; And all the days are chill and drear ; When air and earth are thick with snow, Leaden above and white below; Then let us, as are face the blast, " Give thankslor blessings in the past, And lovingly remember 4 Dear days of sweet September.

When February's sleet and hail Cause men to shiver and to quail; When on the lea and through the snow, Slipping and stumbling, mortals go; Then, as we grumble and complain, Let us, to soothe the biting pain . Of days so dull an'd sober,' Remember bright October.. When March is Felaruary's heir, And snow and slush are everywhere; When fierce winds hustle us about, ,r hopes of Spring to rout; Th„, . • every day . •lessings passed away, •rnA ember That golden, fan' November. When April, foster child of March, Sullen, instead of gay and arch, And giving frowns in place of smiles On agony fresh sorrow piles, Prolonging Winter's gloomy reign; Then let us, as we bear the pain, Look backward, and remember Bright days of mild December.

UNDER A THORN-TREE. Wife, you see I kept them snugly, Our old pictures of langsyne— Old ideals grow often ugly, Not this cottage one of mine— Yours a colour in September— Wife, it seems but yestermom When we sketched, do you remember? Underneath that crimson thorn. - - Yes, that large white owl was near us, In our woodland painting place, Seeming both to see and hear us With an interested face; Looking, oh so wise and woolly, We could fancy he might say, , " Ah, I knew love's phrenzy fully In my young and-heedless day !" Did Sir Robin too deride us , , • Up against that autumn sky, On a tree which could not hide us From his bright and merry eye? "Bob,: you said, "seems sketching boldly in his mind, a larder bare, With us twain both crying coldly, 6 Not a crumb for Bob to spare !' " Then you questioned archly, sadly, "Must love's summer always go? Can it be that love loves madly? Owl and redbreast tell us so • And I drews robin peerizig Through a cottage window-pane, Singing o'er his crumb-feast cheering, "True love's summer does not wane." "Oh, the owl's a cynic, dearest, And a satirist is Rob— Love," I said, "oft sees the clearest All its wealth which none may rob— As to Heaven's Gate we take it, Asking for its blessing there, Love will have a fount to slake it That can keep it fresh and fair." So we left that thorn-tree gaily, Happy-plighted, hand in hand, And our love has since been daily To us twain a summer land. Now the bells of age are tinkled In our ears, my white-haired wife, But though old love grows not wrinkled If its summer is for life. —Good Words for February.

AN ORIGINAL CSRISTIAN NAME.—Not a great many - months ago, a little maiden, born at. West Derby-, Liver-- pool, to the surname of" Pepper," was registered in the following personal names' five-and-twenty in number— viz., Ann, Bertha, Cecilia, Diana, Emily, Fanny, Gertrude, Hy-patia' Inez, Jane, Kate, Louise, Maud, Nora, Ophelia, Quince, Rebecca, Starkey, Teresa, Ulysses, Venus, Wini- fred, Xenophon, Yetty, and Zeus. No doubt the child's father—a laundryman—aimed at originality in confer- ring these designations; and he,must be allowecito have hit it.—"GoodlVords" for February. Another lesson we may receive from the leaf—that of its death. If ever, in autumn, a pensiveness falls upon us as the leaves drift by in their fading, may 'we not wisely, look up in hope to their mighty monuments. Be- hold how fair, how far prolonged, in arch and aisle, the avenues of the valleys, the fringes of the hills, so stately, so eternal ; they are but the monuments of those poor leaves that flit faintly past us to die. -Let them not pass -without our understanding their last counsel .and ex- ample, that we also may build our monument in the world—monuments by which men may remember not where we died, but where we lived.—Ruskin. SELF-IHPROVEMENT.—Nothing is so sad as the cry, "I am useless'?" Happily none need ever be so. A kind word, a gentle act, a modest demeanour, a loving smile, are as so many seeds that we can scatter every moment of our lives, and which will always spring up and bear fruit. Happy are those, who have many around them;. they are rich in opportunities, and may sow plenteously. As self-sacrifice is the basis and essence of virtue, so those virtues are the most meritorious that have cost the greatest effort to attain. Do not look with so much pride on this collection of virtues, but rather bring your- self to account for your faults. Take just one the first that comes, impatience, sloth, gossip, uncharitableness sulkiness, whatever it may be, and attaek-it bravely: It will take at least a month, calculated upon three vic- tories every day, not indeed to eradicate it—a fault is not so short-lived—but to prevent its attaininea dominion over you. That one subdued, then take anothet. It is the work of a lifetime. "Happy should I think-myself," said one, "if I could rid myself of my imperfections but on-i quarter of an hour previous to my death." Men woukl give gold sometimes to buy back a passionate word, and we know of nothing that so destroys unity as the exchange of evil language, especially in the moment of strife. WHAT IS A POUND STERLING ?—This question was asked of Sir Robert Peel in the House of Commons, and he replied by pitching a sovereign to the querist. No better answer is possible. Some years ago, when teach- ing political economy at University College School, I presented to my pupils a curious problem, as follows : Our currency is all based on the sovereign, and the sov- ereign, as defined by Act of Parliament, is 1-1,869 of 40 lbs. troy. . or, otherwise stated, anybody taking ingots of stan- dard gold to the Mint may have them coined without charge into sovereigns, at the rate of 1,869 for every 40 pounds troy; these 1,869 weighing 40 pounds, the same as the ingot gold. This being the case, what is the troy weight of each sovereign? I offer the same problem to any readers. Those who attempt to work it out will find that they have to face a problem something like squaring the circle. I have gone as far as thirteen places of decimals, showing the weight of a sovereign to be nearly 123-2744783306537 grains. How much further one might go without arriving at the actual weight I cannot say. The simplest attainable vulgar fraction is 123 171-623 grains. Nothing could be clumsier than this. It has caused volumes to be written by currency paracloxers, who have denounced the abomination of fix- ing the price of gold. Why, say they, should we not have free trade in gold? Why should the Government arbitrarily fix its price at £3 17s. 100. per ounce in- stead of allowing supply and demand to fix the price of this commodity as of other things? Had the weight of the sovereign been a simple fraction of an ounce, say one-quarter of an ounce, this question would have an- swered itself at once by showing that because four sov- ereigns weigh one ounce the value of gold measured by sovereigns (i.e., its price) must be £4 so long as the weight of the coin remains unchanged and no charge is made for stamping it. It. is the present complex frac- tion that has obscured this very simple subject.— W. atant Williams, in the Gentleman's Magazine. Tun BLENHEIM RAPHAEL—The fact that an absolutely unprecedented price—£70,000—is, subject to the sanc- tion of Parliament, to be paid by the National Gallery for the picture, has aroused general wonderment; though the proposed purchase has on the whole, been hailed with general pride and satisfaction. It cannot too often be repeated that, unprecedented though the price may be, the opportunity is also unique, and cannot under any conceivable circumstances recur. Most of the great maaters are still splendidly represented in the private galleries of Great Britain and elsewhere; but of -Raphael's greater and more representative works there are few or none—save the" Madonna Ansidei "—which have not already found a place in public galleries, where they must irrevocably remain fixect Almost the only other important altar-piece of the same type is the some- what similar but far inferior, " Madonna of the Nuns of St. Antonio "—the so-called "Madone d'un Million." No., doubt several authentic and exquisite works of Raphael axiet, as is well known, in the Bridgewater Gallery, and in the collections of Lord Dudley, Lord Cowper, and the Due d' Aumale ; but none of these have the importance or representative character of the work now under con- alderation. It would have been an everlasting disgrace to the nation, an offence to every art-loving Englishman, if the "Madonna Ansidei," so long a possesion of a great Englsh house, and made additionally precious by its association with a great English name had been allowed to become the chief ornament of the 'Berlin Gallery, or the boast of some private collection.—Claude Phillips in "The Magazine of Art," Trig MDR, Whiz WORLD.—Senor A. de La E. The steamer was stopped, and preparations were made to save him, viben he was heard exclaiming, "Go ahead with your old steamboat! I'll walk behind." "Madam," said a husband to his young wife in a little altercation, which will spring up in the best-regulated families, "when a man and his wife have quarrelled, and each considers the other at fault, which of the two ought to advance towards a reconciliation?" The better- natured and wiser of the two," said the wife putting up her mouth for a kiss, which was given with an unction. She was the conqueror. "WANTED, A WIFE."—Tho clerk to the Kingston-on- Thames Board of Guardians has reported to that author- ity that since the publication of the letter which had been received from a soldier at the Cape; in which the writer asked that a woman might be sent out to him, as he was anxious to get married, no less than 192 applieations had reached his office. Many of these applications, it is sta.' 51, were' "written in tender imitation of the genuine lan- guage of confiding love, and were accompanied with portraits, or with glistening and well pomated locks of hair, ruthlessly cut off as offerings to an unknown affection, and as a tempting guarantee of feminine charms. Some, on the other hand, were business-like and matter-of-fact, but all breathed a desire for matri- monial life."—The board, having received the clerk's report, passed on to the next business without comment. OLD LAMPS AND NEW.—The celebrities of twenty years ago are in these days not nearly so accomplished as the rank and file. They have name in their favour; but it , was won with achievement now easily surpassed by men ' who are only units in a crowd. Something like a re- naissance has been in action about them and its opera- tion has left them far to rearward. They have been neither learning nor forgetting; they have been simply producing; and their appearance among - their juniors —the figure they cut in the mellay which by rights they should order and command—is a little pathetic. They come forward as the champions of old ideals, the ex- ponents of the methods discarded and condemned, the heroes of an achievement already old-fashioned and out of date. New influences have been at work, and they have taken no heed of them; new roads have been opened up, and they have preferred the old; new pro- cesses, new aims, new models have come into vogue, and they have stuck resolutely to their own. In art to pause from learning is to pause from doing, not to ad- vance is to recede. Whitman's profession of duty, "We do but level that lift, to pass and 6ontinue beyond," is more tme...ef liar artist than of any other worker. The presort pallet* has (it may be) as little to say as the generatioeithat went before; but it has been learning while its predecessor has been refraining from new know- ledge, and what it has to say is so much better said than its elder's utterances as to seem of tenfold greater value. The Magazine of Art. Tiny. Yortx PREACHERS.—Ainericans speak of-Wash- ington as the "city of magnificent distances," Phila- delphia is the "city of brotherly love," New York is the "Empire City," Brooklyn the "city. of churches." New York might well contend with her sister city on the other side of the East River for the last title. A view of Manhattan Island from one of the high roofs "down town" embraces an almost bewildering number of spires, and towers, and pinnacles belonging to the churches with which the "Empire City ' is so plentifully siip- plied. Right up the central line gf the island, from Trinity to Central Park, a long To% -of stately edifices mark out the great avenues of trade and residence. All the denominations are supplied with large and well-fur- nished buildings. Every kind of architectural form finds its representative, the most common being some variety of the Gothic, .The churches impress a stranger with the comfort-61 their appointments. They are large, de- corated luxuriously fitted. No expenditure of wealth is, spared to make the Route of God beautiful and plea- sant. Eveci the plainest church belonging to some coloured counnunity is " upholstered " with carpets and cushions. None can complain in New York churches that the inconveniences of the place of worship are such as to be an excuse for non-attendance. Well warmed, well ventilated, well cushioned, well lighted, American churchea invite all by their luxury -and ease. The pul- pit of New York is strong. In all the churches there are clergymen of piety, learning, and eloquence. No city in the world has a higher order of preaching.—The Quiver. BAILIE MIDDLETON'S CANTASS.—It has been questioned whether the majority of women who have received the municipal franchise are grateful for the privilege thereby granted to them. The story of Bailie Middleton's can- vass will show how the measure may yet become popu- lar in a way that its promoters never contemplated. The Bailie was a bluff, good-natured bachelor, somewhere about forty years of age, and was one of the most re- spected citizens of the Scottish burgh of —. He had been a Town Councillor for several years, and had lately been elected to the magistrates' bench. Some weeks before the election of 1882 a solicitor intimated that he would contest the seat so long held by Bailie Middleton and the Bailie knew that, if he wished to retain it, he must personally canvass every voter. Briskly he steps from door to door, smiling and joking with every one he meets. He is receiving more pledges than he at first anticipated, arid consequently he is in the best of spirits. He has only one more voter to call upon and, as he adjusts his eyeglasses over his nose and reads the name on his roll, his face assumes a somewhat contemplative express*, "Janet—Janet Laidlaw," he mutters to himself. "Surely the name is familiar." And as he muses he recalls some forgotten episodes in his life. In a vague way he remembers that he was intimately ac- quainted with a Janet Laidlaw years ago. In fact they had been sweethearts. For many months he had been a devoted worshipper at Janet's shrine, but in consequence of some slight misunderstanding between them a lover's , quarrel took place, and, as the Bailie had been a high- spirited lad in those days, he would never be the first 'to break the ice' " Pshavz ! " he mutters, smiling at the remembrance of his youthful romance. Then he gave the door-bell a vigorous pull in order that its ring might drive this romantic non-sense out of his head. Bailie Middleton was ushered into a room where sat a woman, still very comely, although she could hardly be called young. The Bailie merely glanced her as he entered, but it needed no second look to convince him that the woman before him' and his old sweetheart were one and the same. Miss Laidlaw rose as he entered, shook hands with her visitor somewhat nervously, motioned him to a chair, and then resumed her seat. Of course, the Bailie knew that if he wished to secure Janet's vote he must first make himself as agreeable as possible, consequently he began to talk about everything he thought likely to interest her, and it was natural their conversation should drift back to old times and acquaintances of long ago. The name of one of JaneVilkold friends having been mentioned, the • Bailie had some trouble in bringing her to his remem- brance, when Janet volunteered to show him her friend's likeness, which she had in her album. Of course, it was then natural that the Bailie should ask permission to in- spect Janet's stock of photos, and, of course, Janet gra- ciously granted the request. Then the Bailie drew his chair close to Janet's side, and he turns over the pages of the album, while Janet tells him the name and other particulars regarding the likenesses. But what has brought the Bailie to such a sudden stop? and why does Janet shyly turn away and gaze into the fire? On the page before him the Bailie sees his own photograph, taken while he was a lad in his teens, while opposite him there is a likeness of Janet, which he remembers was taken at the same time. As he gazes on these photo- graphs the timepiece over the fireplace strikes ten, and the Bailie thinks that now is a favourite time to ask if his companion will vote for him at the approaching egc- tiort ! "Janet," he says, "of course you know what has brought me here to-night ?" Although not quite sure, Janet thought she had a pretty good idea of what had brought him thither. She, innocent woman, knew no- thing of the privileges that had been conferred on women by recent legislation. She had not the slightest idea that women had now the same privileges as the lords of the creation in municipal elections, and she . never dreamed for a moment that Bailie Middleton' had come to ask for her vote. She thought he had come on a very different errand. She fancied the Bailie had now realised that it was net good for a man to live alone, and that, in short, he had come to ask her to share his lot. "I have come to ask a favour from you," continued the Bailie. " I want y-ou to pledge yourself to me." "Pledge' myser !" said Janet, gazing on her old sweet- heart with the rekindled fires of true love lighting up her eyes. "Pledge mysel' ! 'Deed will I that, Bailie, an' ye hardly need to ask me to do that" "Thanks, Miss Laidlaw, said the Bailie, with an effort of dignity. "Oh, Bailie! oh John," said Janet, casting a reproachful look at the magistrate, "I see ye havena forgetten my name. Dinna be feared to offend me by ca'in' me "Janet" " Weel, Janet," continued the Bailie, "I may say there's no- a man in the teen 'ill attend to yer interests like my- sel'." "I ken that, John. Oh, you were aye a couthie, thochtful man, an' it was a bad day for us baith that ill-tongued dashers separated us." "But Janet—Miss Laidlaw !" cried the now dumbfounded Bailie. "My 1 good woman, I have come here simply to solicit " Jjeohhnn,," apnu, t mit; hJeaanrett.aian"golwii, ,ft ;k,ena nydo hsai lee. "ThereM "'Rani's', threw herself into the Bailie's arms, and—yes, actually kissed him. "Oh, John. John !" she cried, "I —I hae lo'ed ye a' slang, and noo ye hae made me the happiest woman in a' braid Scotland." What could the Bailie do? As he looked into those loving and confiding eyes up- raised to his, he thought it would be cruel to undeceiVe her. And he never did so. Before many weeks had passed Janet had become Mrs. Middleton,

RACKLEENTINO WITH A VENGEANCE.—What do you *stlaitik,ota landlord who gives his factor full liberty to extrad. whit, rent he chooses, promising to share with him whatever he can ket in excess of existing rents?' Not much! Yet such an arrangement has actually been made between a landlord and his factor in Shetland, with the result that the rent-roll has leaped up twenty- five per tmilirres cent—Echo. T BROTHER AS A LANDOWNER.—There is a good deal of talk current in the Meanie, as to the Feat extent of land held by Sir Thomas Gladstone, Bart., in his own hands. He holds at present no Mayer than thirteen farms, comprising about 3,000 acres of arable land, and it is understood that another of his tenants has intimated his intention of availing himself of a break in his lease and throwing up his holding. THE FARMERS ON LORD BRADFORD'S ESTATE at Black- rod, near Bolton, have determined to resist the payment of tithes. There has recently been an agitation amongst them for the lessening of their burdens, and previous to the tithe audit on Monday they had a meeting and re- solved not to partithes until a reduction of 25 per cent. was made in the rents. .This resolution was agreed to unanimously. LORD Hu-crocus aro ms TENAN'TRY.—Lord Kintere, in reply to a request by his tenantry for a reduction of their rents, says that it is out of his power to comply. He has expended £41,000 on the improvement of his estate, chiefly for the benefit of the tenants, and were he to comply with their request his income would be gone. He adds that he had been content to live on half the in- come of his predecessors. AGEICDT:ItTRAL EDUCATION IN FRANCE.—WhiIe Mr. Chamberlain and others are talking about free educa- tion, it is appropriate- to refer to a new School of Agri- culture and Viticulture, opened at Beaune, France, on the 15th inst. A first-rate education in practical and theoretical agriculture and viticulture is to be given there for £2O a year for boarders, £lO for day boarders, and £2 for day pupils who do not receive any board. The regulations of the school are fully described in the last bulletin issued by the French Ministry of Agricul- ture. There are many such excellent institutions in France, and it is possible that in some remote period, when we have a real Department of Agriculture, some- thing of the kind may be attempted in this country: Farmers will not mind paying rates for free education if their own children can obtain a share of the advan- tages. TREATMENT OF EWES IN LAMB.—Question: HOW should I feed my ewes' which are heavy in lamb? wish to have them in good condition, so that they may have plenty of milk and have strong lambs. Up till now they have been having a very small allowance of turnips, and have had plenty of foggage with a little hay since the new year. Should I now increase the roots, and give any additional food P—Answer Until after lambing, the roots need not be increased to any great *extent, but the addition of a mixture of some more con- centrated food would be useful. A good mixture would be lb. or Vb. of crushed oats, 11b. of bran, with 21bs. ca. 31bs. of cut straw. ° Some would prefer to give oats and linseed cake in equal quantities. The mixture recom- mended by Mr. E. Riley, an experienced Yorkshire farmer, was, for a flock of 200 ewes for the season, tons of linseed cake, 1 tons of oats, 1 ton beans, 1 ton locust bean meal, 1 ton of malt coombs,:B bushels of ',halt, and liewt. common salt. Cabbages are very suitable for ewes. A good load may be given to every 100 ewes daily. EXTRAORDINARY WOOL SEASON AT PORT ADELAIDE.— The Adelaide Observer says :—From the commencement of the present wool season in August last up till now (the end of November), the increase in the number of bales brought to Port Adelaide over the receipts of pre- vious years has been so enormous as to deserve special comment. The causes of this tremendous influx are variously described. Several autherities unanimously point to one, which, I think, is a fair subject for con- gratulation by the colony generally. That is that farmers who for a long time were content to restrict themselves to wheat-growing have within the last year or two added wool-growing to that Industry. Their produce comes down in small lots, it is true, and the appearance of the wool, both with regard to quality and the manner of its packing, will not yet bear comparison with the outputs of the large sheds, but with experience the difference will be less perceptible. So much for the accumulation of the small parcels. Another and per- haps the chief cause of the increase is that our "silent highway," the Murray and its tributaries, have offered much meter opportunities for transit this year than for some time past. WHO ARE THE GAINERS BY THE IMPORTATION OF Foasierk MEAT P—Will You permit me to call your atten- tion to a few facts and figures connected with the pro- fits of middlemen which, I think, ought to be placed before the public. I have lately examined the butchers' bills of two of my neighbours in this county for two different periods—part of 1882 and the end of lElB4—and find the prices charged by the butchers were exactly the same two years ago as now. Now, sir, look at the pro- ducers' side. In 1882, for a barrener weighing 9st. 71bs. I obtained £2 us. 10d. ; last month, for a sheep of simi- lar weight and quality, I obtained £1 17s. 00. In 1882, for a wether teg weighing 9st.llbs., I obtained £2 16s. 404 this month, for a sheep of similar weight and quality, I obtained £2 6s. 11d. A statement like this demands little comment. The butcher obtains a reduce Von in price in the first case of 14s. 90., and in the second of 9s. 50., in which advantage the consumer does not participate. If, then, the butcher considered the profit he obtained two years ago adequate—and that he did so we have no reason to doubt—clearly the pre- sent reduction which he obtains from the producer is 14s. 9i41. and 9s. 54-d. respectively per sheep of exces- sive profit. THE Smite Holds STUD Boox.—The sixth volume of the stud book of the Shire Horse Society, containing the pedigrees of 785 stallions and 1,121 mares, the numbers of the stallions ranging from (3,412) to (4,196) has been issued. Illustrations of the champion- stallion and mare at the London Show, 1884, are included in this volume, together with the champion mares of 1882 and 1883, taken from life by Mr. Samuel Carter, jun. It was the intention of the Council to have included the whole of the champion mares of the society's shows, but un- fortunately those gaining that high distinction in 1880 and 1881 are dead, and no photograph or painting of them is extant. Stallions and mares which have been previously registered can be re-entered for the purpose of showing the prizes and awards you by them since their first entry, but in the re-entry of stallions they must in all cases retain their original stud book number. The report of the London Show, 1884, written by Mr. Sanders Spencer, is given in this volume, together with • the awards of the prizes, their re-issue in the stud book having been considered advisable for preservation and for future reference. It is stated in the preface that in future volumes stallions cannot be entered under names appearing in preyious editions. For example, no stallion can be entered as Honest Tom' he can only be accepted as Honest Tom sth or Honest Tom 6th; and the same with What's Wanted can only be entered as What's Wanted 2nd, &c. ENSILAGE Y. CONDENSED Mmx. —Would the Anglo- Swiss Condensed Milk Company tell us what is the dif- ference between the milk of silage-fed cows, of which they complain, and that from cows suitable for conden- sing? I have seen reports in American papers of a similar character against the use of silage, but from the analysis of the silage and the mode it was given to cows, otherwise could not be expected, for the silage contained an excess of acetic acid, whilst the cows were fed too exclusbzely on this imperfectly-made silage, which had, as we read the Americarl chemical reports, undergone the secondary fermentation to a large extent. Lactic acid is the natural acid of silage, and-the practical ques- tion is to make it with such only, or with a minimum of acetic acid. Farmers must remember that in making silage they have to pay an apprentice fee, as in other branches of agriculture, and that much has to be learned in making silage and feeding milch cows and other live stock of the farm with it. But, if proper attention is paid, healthy much cows will give better milk, when properly fed on well-made silage, than when Lfed on roots, ml-eake, and the other articles now used. What London and other large towns want is a sufficient supply of rich milk at a price that will drive condensed milk out of the market. This is obviously what is looming in the distance, let the milk-preserving companies, American and English, say as they may to the:contrary. We have tried these preserved milks to tea and coffee, and also to strawberries, &c., but prefer what the dairy- man supplies.—W. 8., in Agricultural Gazette. HOW' THEY SUCCEED'IN CHEST/la.—A Cheshire agri- culturist writes :—When they do succeed, it is by hard work, thought, and courage. Nearly all the successful ones say it is by hard work alone. Muscle wins the day, if it ever is won; and when the daily life of a Cheshire farmer is followed, much truth will be found in the statement, and more still if that of his wife and women-folk is followed. He rises at 4 o'clock a.m. in summer, and 5 o'clock in winter; and during the calv- ing season he is up all night for from 20 to 50 nights, -according to the number of his dairy cows. He works until six o'clock when there is daylight until that hour, then he milks (another hdur's work), and after that he "gardens a bit." In hay harvest from 5 a.m. to 7 p.m. are the normal hours, and in corn harvest the same, only longer in both cases when." carrying," and especi- ally if there be a moon to supplement the daylight. The wife rises as early and sometimes before her husband to top or cream the milk of the previous night; to turn her cheese under press and in the room'; to receive the morning's milk as it comes, fresh from the shippons, into the cheese-tub or vat; to regulate its temperature' by heating or cooling; putting it together, and adding the rennet to it; when, for an hour, she may partake of breakfast; and if she be a young wife, she must wash the baby and get his older brothers or sisters ready for school. Then, with a diligence that admits of no delay and no looking away, she makes the cheese and gets the dinner ready; after which she may, go a little slower, except on washing and churning clays, until tea-time, when milking-time comes again; the day ending with a fear of something being left over until to-morrow that should have been done to-day, and a repeating of the truism that "women's work" on a dairy farm "never is done." For half-a dozen or a dozen times during the year, a short respite may be taken in the afternoons, by a visit to some relative and a chat round the tea table, or even a visit to some public tea meeting; but that is

CAN FARMING BE arAns va FAT ?—Mt. J. Scott Bankes, "Soughton_liall, Northopanintshire, writes to a contem- porary.:L=ln endeavouring to set before the public the financial management of my Arm for the last 24 years, I can vouch for the correctness of my figures, and can state that I . have endeavoured to farm on tenants prices, avoiding extravagance on the one hand and on the other availbag.myself of every opportunity of sea- son, &c., to bring the land in my occupation to the highest state of fertility. My farm is 210 acres in extent of which 82 are old park land, which is much im- poverished by the timber growing on it, and the expense of fertilising it is greatly increased by the gathering of Iseveral scores of loads of leaves fallen during the autumn. The land lies about 400 feet above the level, and is described by Mr. Rigby, secretary to the Liver- pool and Manchester Society, when going over it in 1883, in the following terms :—‘Mr. J. Scott Bankes is hin- dered by the boundaries of his farm from lbringing it into the best shape as a mbdel prize farm, andlts high- lying position and poorer soil limit its productiveness; but little, if any, fault can be found with the manage- ment." I may add, the subsoil is sand and gravel, and the land is all thoroughly drained. The rent I have charged myself throughout is Zl. per acre; the total capital I ,have laid out on the land is £l,OOO, or about £5 per acre. I now give the totals of expenditure and receipts for the years 1881 to 1884 inclusive, and in the last year I have thought it ctesirable to give each item by which the total amount is arrived at : • _ id _ _ . .

£1361 2 41 £1543 3 7 I have just had my farm produce, stock, Su.. valued as to an incoming tenant, by an independent valuer; his estimate is £2,550, being £1,550 in excess of capital laid, out This sum; added to the £2,354 of 'income over eur penditure makes the total gain £3,900 in 24 years, which is a percentage on capital of 16 per cent, for the whole period; added to which there is a guinea a week for bailiff's wages which a tenant farmer occupying the same amount Of land would not require, he himself dis- charging the bailiff's duties, and these wages amount to 5 per cent, per annum. For the satisfaction of my 'readers, I would say the regular labour employed are a bailiff and his wife, the latter making the butter and rearing the poultry, one cowman, one shepherd, !two" carters, one labourer,. and one boy. The live stock on my farm at present are —5 horses, 2 colts, 44 cattle 134 sheepl2 pigs, 25 couple of poultry, 3 ducks. I ;rust this statement which I certify to be correct will cause the tenant farmers of this neighbourhood to believe that sufficient capital judiciously laid out on land is not so bad an investment as is generally believed. I owe my success, if success my undertaking be deemed,-to speedy sales, quick returns, the services of an honest and intelligent bailiff, and a clever and hardworking shepherd.

Should it be desirable to put in any cuttings of goose- berry or currant trees they ought to be put in with all speed. As a rule cultivators select any pieces from Bin. to 12in. in length; they move all the buds from that portion that is to be buried in the ground, leaving about three buds above the soil, the terminal being trained up- right. We prefer to leave one or two more, as in case of accident to one, the :foundation of the tree would be one-sided after a shoot is to be taken for a leader, unless ultimately the:shoots are reduced to one, and this is al- lowed to throw side shoots the following season. Even- with this expedient one season may be said to have been lost. If the eyes are not nibbled or picked out from the portion that enters the soil they give much trouble by producing a number of suckers annually. It should however be noted that though nursetymen and others adopt this single stem system, suet' plants are shorter lived on dry gravelly soil than those that had a fair number of buds left to produce suckers. Obviously this is because if a branch dies a sucker can be intro- duced into its place. It is not necessary to devote an open or sunny position to the Cuttings, as they do much better in a partly-shaded and sunless one. We usually plant them with the spade, and after the line is stretched we hold the spade perpendicularly and bring it down so as to cut close to the line and, if possible, to the depth of eight inches. If this depth is not attained by the first stroke it is readily reached after the ground is marked, as the soil, the width of the spade, should be taken out and conveyed to where it is likely to be convenient for Ithe purpose of filling up after the cuttings are all in. In the bottom of this channel an inch or two deep of sand ' should be placed for the base of the cuttings to rest upon which will induce them to- form roots. With one hand the cuttings are taken and placed against the bank made when the soil was cut down, and the other is en- gaged in pressing soil against the cuttings to sustain them in their place, until more can be placed with the spade and the pressure of the foot brought to bear on them. After the ground is filled in and made level to about 10 inches in width, we stretch the line about eight inches from the first row and proceed to-make another cut. This is much more easily accomplished than the first one. In light sandy soils theVntroduction of sand is unnecessary, and the trenches or :channels need not be more than six inches deep. The distance between the cuttings in the row should be about three inches, pro- viding t is intended to move them the first year after they have rooted. THE FRONT GARDEN.—In looking over some Clematis we discovered that they had commenced growing. This Irather surprised us, seeing that the weather has not been of a character to produce young growth. We conclude' that the Prowtli must Ivry@ bean made befell gig frost. - . • and that old leaves that still hant Oh, is well as some small shoots, had provided protection, as well as being in a measure responsible for this incipient growth. Not wishing to encourage it, we moved the superfluous shoots as well as the decayed leaves, so as to expose the buds as much as possible. The main shoots were left undisturbed for the present. AU newly-planted subjects or cuttings of such things as Pansies Carnations, and Pinks should be examined, as in all probability they will be found much disturbed by the frost, when they must be pressed in again. Bush or dwarf Roses are extremely liable to get loose at the collar, and a hole will be ap- parent round the stem. This should be closed in, or it will act as a conductor of water, which would prove most mischievous if the frost returned. THE WiNnow.—Hyacinths: When the root of those grown in glasses approach the bottom of .the glass they should be brought gradually to the light and cautiously guarded from currents of cold air. If the roots do not look healthy, or if the water has an offensive odour it should be emptied, and the glass filled with some fresh rain or Soft water, which should stand in the room till it becomes of the some temperature as that which has been in use. If the roots are not too numerous they , may be pulled out and washed. Should the process be at all risky, much may be done by, pouring two or three lots of water into the glass and stake it well each time before emptying. Pieces of charcoal will be of much service in preserving the water sweet. Hyacinths in pots will require td be examined, though with the cold weather we have had, the growth should not be very far advanced on those outside 'covered with ashes. But those that may have been stored in cupboards or cellars will be more advanced. Han inch long they should be brought to the light and have a paper hood placed over them for a few days if they are placed at once in the window. As one-fourth of the soil, will be permeated by roots it must not be allowed to get dry.

"You may speak," said a fond mother, "about people having strength of mind, but when it comes to strength of don't mind, my son William surpasses everybody I ever knew." "Have you," asked the judge of a recently-convicted man, "anything to offer the Court before sentence is passed 2" "No, your honour," replied the prisoner; "my lawyer took ray leo farthing." • A little girl, who wtfs accustomed to the plainest style of living, having been taken to dine with a.rich friend, described the dinner in the folloWing terms :--" Oh! such a time we had; there were four dinners all after one smother."

" Don't you think you have a good mamma, to spread such nice large slices of bread and jam for you ?" said an old lady to a little boy who was enjoying his tea." " Yes " was the reply; "but she would be still better if she'd let me spread the jam on myself." WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. The second quarterly meeting of this Council was held in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall, on Tursday even- ing, the Mayor (Alderman, Harrison) in the chair. There were also present Aldermen Pickmere, Chandley, Holmes, Webster ; Coutfcillors Greening, Burgess, Wright, Dakin, Bolton, Dixon Barker, Mackie, Ashton, Fleming, Brown, Dakin, Marsh, J. Pierpoint, Tinsley, Francomb, Milner, Roberts, Broadbent, Hutchinson, Whittle, Sutton, Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), Chorley (borougb treasurer), and Longdin (borough surveyor). PRINCE ALBERT VICTOR. Amongst the Mayor's communications was a copy of an address sent by the Mayor and Town Clerk "To his Royal Highness Prince Edward of Wales, K.G.," congratulating him on the attainment of his majority; and also a copy. of the reply which had been received from his Royal High- ness.

Councillor 11,facitna commented upon the young Prince having been given the title of "Prince Edward of Wales" in the address, whilst his proper name was "Albert Victor," the name with which he had himself signed his.own reply. Lie (Dr. Mackie) thought this mistake in the address ought to be corrected, and he pledged the Council his word that there was no constituted authoritr in .the country, and no newspaper, except the Times, which did not give the Prince the name of Albert Victor.

_ The MAYOR pointed out that the address had gone and could not be recalled, and the matter dropped. • THE LAMPS.—BRIDGE•STREET IMPROVEMENT. The &met Improvement and Lighting Committee re- corded that the sum of £2,700, inclusive of £lO per cent., , but exclusive of legal charge, be paid to Messrs. Skelton for the.purchase of their property in Bridge-street.—Also that the surplus land in Bridge-street be sold by public auction as soon as practicable, and that the Town Clerk be instructed! to prepare the condition of sale; and, further, that the buough eurvevor be instructed to prepare a block plan of , the surp'us lard in Bridge-street to be re-sold by the Cot- pore ion. Councillor Drum moved and Councillor !Lusa seconded, the adoption of these minutes. Alderman WEBSTER called the attention of the Committee to a lamp in Horsemarket-street which was in a very awk- ward position. Alderman PICKMERE referred to a lamp placed near the Central Station in such a position that he was given to understand that alrdady three brougham doors had been seriongly injured by it. Councillor TINSLEY confirmed Alderman Pickmere's re- marks. Some members of his own family had had their brougham door damaged by this lamp, and be believed he could mention two other instances of a similar kind. Councillor J. PlERPoterr said he had on two or three occasions complained to the committee about the position of a lamp at Bevesey. This lamp could not be more in the way than it was. Councillor BARKER thought that Mr. Plerpoint's diffi- culty was that he could net drive straight round a corner. (Laughter.) He had himself proposed that that lamp should be where it was, and he was proud that motion was =tied. As far as the lamp at the Central Station was concerned, it should have the attention of the committee.

Councillor Dixote was in favour of the lamp at Bewsey remaining where it was. Councillor GREBNING said he had not before heard any complaints about the lamp referred to by Alderman Webster, but he had with regatel to the one at the Central I Station. He had heard complaints about the lamp in Bew- sey repeatedly; Ise never from anybody but Mr. Pierpoint. (Laughter.) The committee had visited the point, and they could not for the life of them see how it could be altered for the better. Councillor J. Przarom : You must have been blind. Councillor MACKIE asked whether the blocks of land in Bridge-street, which had been arranged for sale by the sur- veyor, would be of such limited sizes as to give a fair op. portunity to those who were only the possessors of small SIMS Of money, or whether it was intended to present them In such large blocks as would only enable capitalists or even companies going in for them. Councillor WRIGHT thought that when the plan came before the Council that was intended to be adopted, they would be quite satisfied that everyone should have a chance of buying. Ccuncillor BROADBENT wa9 quite sure the committee would.take stach measures as regarded the sale of this pro- perty, as would in their wisdom tend to secure the best possible prices for the land that was to be sold. The committee's minutes were then passed. MR DINWIDDIE'S SALARY. The Sanitary Committee recommended that the salary of Mr. Thomas Dinwiddie, the manager of the Longford depot be increased to the sum of £2OO per annum, such increase to take effect from the 25th March next.—They had re- solved that the price to be charged for concentrated manure should be as follows until further notice, viz. :—For two tons and upwards, £6 10a per ton ; for less than two tons, £7 per ton. Also that the tender of Mr. John Banner, of Edgeworth-streee, for 24 slops for scavengers at les 10d each, and the tender of Messrs Hall and Son, for 24 hats at 28 10d each according to the sample, be accepted. Counc!llor MILNER proposed the adoption of these minutes. With regard to Mr. Dinwiddie's salary, he said that officer had been engaged at a salary of £l5O. The committee had some difficulty in persuading Mr. Dinwiddie to take the situation as it was a reductien on the salary he bad received for a long time previous. Individual mem- bers of the committee promised him that if he could prove 11 by the work he did at the Longford depot that he had in- creased the output of manufactured manure to such an ex- tent as to justify them in giving him an extra £5O a year, he should have that £5O. The report as to the work at Longford depot was now complete, and would -show that I Mr..Dinwiddie had ftiluiled Us part er the bargain; and that he WAS entitled to the increase of salary. Iu 1982, the year Mr. Dinwiddie was engaged, the total sales amounted I to £1,318 18s 6d, and of concentrated manure to £195 ; in 1883 the total sales were £1,497 Ss Id, and of concentrated manure £589; in 1884 the total sales amounted to £1,670, 4s, and of concentrated manure to £614. The increase had been with the same machinery, and he took it as simply due to the good management of Mr. Dinwiddie. (Hear, hear).

ConncillOr BARKER seconded the motion. Councillor Dixox supported the motion. Last year he had proposed that Mr. Dinwiddie's salary be increased £5O because he believed he was the best man they had ever had at Longford works. If he had more room at the works ho Would he able to increase the production and at a less coat of labour, but the cemmittee in their wisdom placed the ma- chinery in such a position that it was most difficult to work with.

Coneciilcr BOLTON said that rccommendation was the same as that they had before them a year ago, and he could find nothing more to support than there was then. The time to increase the salary would be when the extension of the works had been carried out, and when there was more work to he done. He moved that the minutes be confirmed with the exceptima of that proposal. Councillor WzrrrLE seconded this amendment. He con- sidered there was nothing to do at Longford. They had a foreman who went out into the fields to shoot small birds, and a clerk, a boy, did all the work at the depot. Re asked the Council if theywould do the sante in their, omn busi. Deans ad ;hey proposed to do for the Corporation, He 171'61:14 key "N 0.57 Laugher.) Councillor Mettsrt spoke in favour of the increase. Councillor ROBERTS supported the recommendation of the committee. lie did not think the concentrated wisdom of the Council was vested in Councillor Whittle. (Laugh- ter.) If it were not absurd to treat Councillor Whittle's remarks in anything like seriousness, the raerences he had made to the officers at Longford depot Would be exceedingly cruel and unkind in every sense of the word. If they were In the least degree correct the Council would be guilty of the greatest possible neglect of its duty in paying men who had literally nothing or next to nothing to do. He thought that a man who increased the sales of hie department in two years by £770 was worth considerably more than £5O a year of an advance. 'Councillor BOLTON: It is not all profit. Councillor ROBERTS: The more you produce with the same machinery the larger the increase in the profits. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Wairrix: No, it isn't; the more you make the more you lose. (Laughter.) Councillor ROBERTS said that might be so, according to Councillor Whittle's mathematics, but he would have to be a little more enlightened before he could see it. Mr. Din- widdie hid been promised an increase if he produced certain results; he had produced those results, and he was entitled to the increase. Councillor BrßGEss supported the proposal of the committee.
Alderman PICRMERE said he felt surprised that Coun- cillors Bolton and Wkittle should object to the paltry amount of £5O being added to the salary of a man who was worth far more.

The MAYOR was of opinion that Mr. Dinwiddie richly deserved the amount the committee proposed to give him. Councillor MILNER haying replied, Councillor Bolton's amendment was put to the meeting, when only the mover and seconder (Councillor Whittle) and Councillor Fleming voted in its favour. The minutes were consequently passed by a large majority.

• EATING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE. In the minutes of this committee It was recommended that the sum of £l4B 6a 2d, the apportionment of the cost of laying foundations, kerbing and tiling of Gaskell-street, be approved. The committee had also resolved that Bridge.. street from Friar's Gate to Ryland-street be paved with suit- able Irish sets, and that the sum of £126 15, the cost of laying foundations, kerbing and tiling Bridgewater-street, be approved.

Councillor WRIGHT moved the adoption of these min- utes with the exception of that referring to the paving of Bridge-street, Which, he said the committee had decided to reconsider. Councillor EICTCHINSON seconded. Alderccan WEBSTER and Alderman PICKMERE expressed pleasure at the withdrawal of the minute having reference to Bridge-street, _

I Coun—cillor Dam; said he should have liked to hear the views of Aldermen Webster and Pickmere as to how the street should be paved. Aldernali PICHMERE : With wood. CouncTor DixON was very glad to hear that as he was himself in favour of wood pavement. There was no place where the benefit of wood would be felt so much as in Bridge-street.
_ The mmutes.were then mfirnted. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. Alderman WEBSTER moved thUt the accounts of this cmrnittee, amonnting to £5O 10a 4d, be confirmed, and Councillor FLEMING seconded.

Councillor Bunagss said that the confirmation of the ac- counts Constituted the whole of the business of the commit- tee. He hoped there was nothing else in regard to which it was not intended to give them information. He thought it desirable that the Council should know if the School Attend-1 ance Committee took important action with regard to other matters. Alderman WEBSTER replied that the accounts were all over which the Council had control, and he moved the con- firmation of them. The reason there was no other minute on the paper was that owing to the closing of the school for the holidays there had been no meeting of the committee, but Councillor Burgess would recollect that annually copious reports of the proceedings of the committee were presented, in addition to the monthly report. The accounts were confirmed. MUSEUM, LIBRARY, AND ARTS COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee, which were adopted on Ithe motion of Alderman WEBSTER, seconded by Councillor BURGESS, contained a report from Mr. Owen that in response to an application made by the chairman, the authorities of ' the South Kensington Museum had arranged to lend a col- lection of art objects in four glass cases. The firet exhibit will consist of wrought ironwork, glass, wood carving, and electro-types. The Curator reported that during 1884 the visitors to the Museum numbered 23,184, the volumes issued to subscribers 25,708, and those issued to readers 14,132.

• THE MARKETS EXTENSION. Alderman CHANDLEY moved, and Councillor Hixos seconded, the adoption of the minutes of the Markets Com- mittee, which contained a resolution to the effect that the tender of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, Limited, for iron roof for the markets extension, at £1,017 tis 10d, be accepted. Councillor MACKIE asked if a further extension of the 28 6d a week stalls was intended, and in reply Alderman CRANDLEY said that the new part of the market would be roofed, but it was not yet decided what would ultimately be / done with it. ' The Council might be assured, however, that I stalls for the sale of market produce would be encouraged in preference to stalls for the sale of drapery and dry goods. SHOGEST. D IMPROVEMENTS AT THE BATHS. The Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee recommen- ded that the Borough Surveyor be instructed to prepare a report and plans for the erection of a new bath and altera- tions to the present baths. I Alderman HOLMES asked to what extent it was proposed Ito extend the baths ?

Alderman WEBSTER : There will be plans submitted to the Council before it is done. Councillor BOLTON objected to money being spent on the privileged few. Councillor MAMIE said the Council would bo glad to meet the requirements even of the rich, but if the resoultion would pledge them to the expenditure of a large sum, the sooner they pulled up the better. They had of late decided on large expenditures, and if that was now intended he thought the clause should be expunged for the present. Councillor ROBERTS said that he had had a personal and practical experience of the disgraceful state of the baths at present. Before any money could be expended they would require the sanction of the Council, and he knew enough of building to be aware that they would not be able to do any- thing before 188 d, so that on the ground of economy there need be no hesitation. On sanitary grounds, and on the ground of teaching yoang men and boys to swim, it was time that something should be done at the baths. They were utterly inackquate, dirty in their surroundings, and it was time an improvement was made.

Alderman WEBSTER said that it was an error to say that the baths were for the privileged few. They were for the benefit of the ratepayers at large. (Hear, hear.) Whatever the cost, the baths must be enlarged to meet the demand made upon them.
Aldermen Pickmere and Holmes, and Councillors Green- ing, Broadbent, Whittle, and Dixon having spoken, the minutes were adopted on the motion a the Maxon, seconded by Councillor J. PIERPOINT.

GAS COMMITTEE. On the consideration of the minutes of this committee, Councillor Dixox called attention to the quality of the gas, which he thought would be better if more pure, even though it were of a lees illuminating power. He was prepared to move that the gas be analysed monthly. Alderman HOLMES thought no objection would be made to that being done. He mentioned that of late there had been a large increase in the consumption of gas. The minutes were then passed, on the motion of Alder- man HOLMES, seconded by Councillor GREENING.

THE SALARY OF THE MAGISTRATES' CLERK. A discussion ensuO, on the following letter entered in the minutes of the General Purposes Committee, and the re- commendation accompanying it, viz. :—" I beg respectfully to renew my application for as increase of my salary as Magistrates' Clerk to £5OO a year. I need hardly remind you that this is a self-supporting department, and makes no demand upon the borough rate. The fees earned mere than justify the increase asked for, and if the amount actually received occasionally is below the augmented salary, it arises from the leniency of the magistrates in making re- missions, and the system of the Borongh Treasurer, who Idoes not pay for the work done for the Corporation in cases where the defendants do not pay costs. As you know there are many duties performed to which no fees attach, and the byelaws now under consideration must necessarily add ma- terially to the work of my department."—The recommend- ation was that the salary be increased. • The MAYOR proposed, and Alderman WEBSTER seconded, the adoption of the minutes. Councillor J. PIERPOINT asked where, when the fees amounted to more than £450 a year, now paid to the clerk, the surplus went to. If it went to the borough funds he should oppose the increase, and if necessary move an amend. ment,

Alderman HOLMES said that it was wished to make the salary somewhat approximate to the amount of money re- ceived M fees. There had last year only been a surplus of £7 odd, and it seemed out of the question to give an ad- vance of £5O.

Alderman WEBSTER said it was true that for one year the surplus was so small, but for the last four years it had been more than £2oo—that was £5O per annum. The clerk did a great amount of work for the Corporation for which no fees were charged, and tie did not think the Council could honestly refuse the increase.

Councillor Wntrrtar did not know whether the Corporation funds would be treated the same as private funds, but he thought no individual would ply £5OO for what they could get for £250. He thought the surplus should go to the county and borough funds for paying the police. Coun. MACKIE thought that lengthened services should be recognised, and that the money was well earned. After the manner in which Mr. White had served them for a number of years, to make a point of contention about a salary of £5O was unworthy of them. Alderman PICKBIKRE thought that the magistrates were in favour of the Increase, and he in consequence agreed with it.

Alderman CFUNDLISY thought it was patent to the whole town that the magistrates' clerk performed his duties in a satisfactory, able, and unassuming manner. Warrington had an incteasing population, which meant increased work, and he thought the clerk shotrld in consequence receive more remuneration.

The MAYOR said the clerk could write to the Secretary of State and get the surpltis of thv feee. Councillor PIERPOIRT asked if the clerk would get the whole of the surplus were it to amount to £1,500. He thought not, and he csnsidered that,£4so was a sufficient sum for the duties performed. The Tovric CLERK said that the burgesses were not en. titled to make profit out of the fees. If the fees amounted to more than the salary then the only course was either to Increase the salary or reduce the fees.

Councillor BROADBENT said that took it as a broad ground that they should pay the magistrates' clerk some- where about the amount of the fees. The fees exceeded the salary by £7, and it was his opinion that during the present year they would very likely fall below the salary. But at the same time the minutes had been passed by the com- mittee, and he should feel inclined to support their confir- mation.

Councillor GREENING said that it would be better if Mr. White charged for what he did, and if what had been stated was correct—that he did work to the extent of £l5O per annum for the Corporation—that would raise his salary to SGOO. He thought it should be positively ascertained whether they could not retain any portion of the fees, as he had been told that in other boroughs a certain salary was paid and the clerk did not take the whole of the fees. In answer to Councillor Roberts, the MAYOR said that the magistrates' clerk was not entitled to receive the actual fees himself. It was provided that he should be paid by salary, but that the salary should approach the amount of fees. The clerk being paid by salary, it incidentally occurred that the Corporation business had been done free: inasmuch as Mr. White received a salary no notice had been taken of the extra work.

After further discussion an amendment moved by Coun- cillor Panporwr to the effect that the minutes be con- firmed with the exception of the one referring to the mag- istrates' clerk's salary, was put to the meeting and lost. The original motion was then carried, 16 voting for and 8 against it.

SUNDAY CLOSING. Councillor Bcuarws moved that a petition in favour of Sunday closing be sent to the House of Commons. Many Town Councils had taken the same step and Lancashire ‘Specially had taken a prominent part in the question. He then spoke on the evils of Sunday drinking and the anomaly of the drink trade being permitted when others were not I permitted. I Councillor GREENING seconded the resolution, which was I supported by Councillors Dixon, Tinsley, and Mackie, and Alderman Webster. Councillor BOLTON opposed the resolution, and addressed the Council at length, rematking that Councillor Burgess was afflicted with zeal in favour of the Church of England Association. He (Councillor Burgess) proposed class high'. lation, but liked a glass of beer himself. (Laughter.) He was interested in the grocery trade, and perhaps thought that if less beer was drunk there would be more tea used. He dared say that if a deputation of the grandmothers of Warrington waited upon Councillor Burgess he would help them to stop the sale of toffy bemuse it inade.the children's teeth rot. (Loud laughter.) Mr. Bolton then argued that , where tried Sunday closing had proved a failure. Councillor BROADBENT (interrupting) *id that that state of durance was becoming rather excruciating, And he moved the adjournment of the meeting. The MAYOR: Till when? Councillor BROADBENT : Till the clav on which the next Council meeting is held. Councillor DIXON said he would second that proposition

FOREIGN NEWS. THE SOUDAN CAMPAIGN. RETREAT OF THE ARABS TO BERBER.—OCCUPA- TION OF BERTI. Telegrams from Lord Wolseley : Korti, February Ist, 10-25 a.m.—News from Earle to 7 P.m. January 30th. Has advanced troops to within about seven miles of Birti, but owing to difficulties of river be cannot concentrate force there until to-morrow. He may be ready to attack on 3rd inst. Colonel Butler, who coin- Mands advanced guards, reconnoitered Birti, and found enemy there in'strong position. I hope enemy will stand, as our column is strong. A deserter, lately from Berber, reports a letter just received by enemy's commander at Birti, from Emir at Berber, informing ITim that he had °Coupled Metammeh, and had sent forward by steamer to IChartotm soldiers, cattle and grain. He advised Com- mander not to oppose our advance, and that we were going to send troops and supplies across desert from Korosko to Abu Halamed• He reported the names of some Sheikhs that had been killed in our victory at Abu Kies, and that rumour said Hussein Pasha Khalifa had died in the Mandt's •Cahip. He says there are twesty-six survivors of Stewart'e Party .in Berber. They are Syrians and Greeks. They are het kept prisoners, but cannot leave tbe town. IKamen, FEB. 2ND, 9-20 P ox—Report from Earle, dated ' Yesterday, just received.- He had occupied Birti, which : had been deserted by the enemy. Two uncles of Stile- man, the murderer of Stewart, have come into camp and Made submission. Hussein, tha stoker of Stewart's steamer, has escaped from the enemy and reached Earle's Crnl). River very difficult, but column overcoming all Moetacles. XORTI, MONDAY.—Another deserter has come in from the Arabs at Bull. He says that the Emir of Berber has received a letter from the Mah li. stating that the English are now in communication with Khartoum, and have sent . ,trnuPs and provisions to General Gordon in the steamers. the force of Monassir fighting men intrenched at Berber ....numbers 4,000. It is considered probable that Sir Charles ' wilson will have returned to Metammeh by the 31st ult., in • Which case we ought to hear the result of his visit to Khar- toum before the end of the week —Stamlard. •• Cam°, Srzenay.—The following temporary appointments have been made :—General Sir Herbert Stewart is succeeded Majer-General Sir Redvers Buller, while Sir Evelyn 1 w 00d succeeds Sir Redvers Buller as Chief of the Staff w ith- Lord Wolseley ; Brigadier-General Grenfell succeeds Sir IvelYn Wood as Commander-in-Chief of the Egyptian : IktruY, being replaced by Colonel Clery in command of the ~ Ines of Communication on the Nile. As General Stephen- ' entl is unable to leave Cairo, Major-Gen. Dormer, chief of his , staff, will start to-morrow on a tour of inspection up the -Nil e, Visiting the cataracts. . Clamp, WEDNESDAY.—Lord Wolseley telegraphs from •Rorti that th,e First Battalion of the Royal Irish gained the , °Prize. of £lOO offered by him to the regiment which should , Make the quickest passage from Sarras to Debbeh. , A. Suakim telegram in The Times says Colonel Chertnside • gla arrived. The Tribe sent through him a convoy of tnels to Kassala. The rebels attacked the convoy, : te:hich lost fifty men, killing 250. Five thousand Abyssi- e. 'garrison,. n'all troops have been sent to assist the Galabet and Geerah ,

At a committee meeting of the British Football Associa- tion held at the Bay Horse, Blackburn, on Monday evening, a sub-committee was appointed to go through the English Association rules, for the purpose of suggesting amendments to be made at the annual meeting. The question of allow- ing membets of clubs in the Asseciation to play for clubs who did not belong the Association was consilered, arwl generally disapproved, but no definite arrangement was 'arrived at. A letter was read from the Aston Villa Club favourable to the legalisation of professionalism, and suggest- ing that a conference be held, with the object of bringing about its legalisation. All present spoke in strong condem- nation of the action of certain clubs continuing to figure as amateurs, when it was easy of proof that the contrary was the case. The Association are hopeful that the recognition of professionalism will soon be established.

div.head: OUFRIGES.
div.p: OUFRIGES.

Naw YORE, MONDAY.—The four men who were arrested in connection with the explosion in Grand-street, New York, yesterday, have been discharged. One of them states that he saw under the windows of the room, in the stove used by the employes en strike, a tin can, with a coil of cotton cord attached that was splattering like a fuse. The association to which the men on strike belong ex- presses indignation at the imputation that day were the authors of the outrage. THE PRINCE OF WALES. PARIS, WEDNESDLE.—The Prince of Wales left here yesterday evening for Cannes, where His Royal Highness will remain till the 17th, returning to London on the 19th. CANNES, WEDNESDAY.—The Princa of Wales arrived here at three o'clock this afternoon, and was received at the railway station by the Prince and Princess of Saxe- Meiningen. PORTUGAL AND THE CONGO.

LISBON, WEDNESDAY.—In to-Clay's sitting of the Cham- ber of Deputies the Minister of the Colonies said, in reply to a question whet'uer the news from London with regard to the seizure of the Lower Congo by Portugal was true, that he was without any information on the subject, but that the Governor of Angra Pequena pcsseseed sufficiently wide instructions to cause the rights of Portugal to be re- spected. BLOWING TIP OF A CHURCH WITH DYNAMITE. BERLIN, THURSDAY.—Particulars from St Petersburgh regarding the recent burning of the Greek Orthodox Church at Jacosptrdt, Courland, state that the edifice was blown up by dynamite. A strict inquiry has been instituted by the authorities, but up to the present has not led to the arrest of the guilty parties.

div.head: O'DONOVAN ROSSA SHOT BY A
div.p: O'DONOVAN ROSSA SHOT BY A
WOMAN.

NEW YORK, MONDAY EnsDra.—This afternoon, at about a quarter past five, while O'Donovan Rossa was walking down Chambers•street, he was approached by a handsome young woman, quietly dressed, wearing spectacles, who pre- sented the appearance of an intellectual school teacher. On nearing him she drew from the pocket of her dress a five. chambered revolver, of small calibre and, presenting it, tired one shot at him. Rossa threw up 'his arms, exclaimed, "I am shot," and fell heavily on the pavement. A large crowd assembled round the spot where Rossa lay, and several people followed the woman and arrested her. The man who actually apprehended her said he found her in the street brandishing a weapon. She was conducted to the police-station, and behaved with remarkatie calmness. A man who entered the station with her informed the police that she had just shot a man. The sergeant asked, "Do you know the man?" and she replied with a slight English accent, "Yes, I shot O'Donovan Rossa." he looked de- mure as she stood at the bar, and betrayed no excitement. She gave her name as Yeslet Dudley, and said she was a native of England, and hospital nurse by occupation. She described herself as a widow of 24, but did not appear more than 18. Subsequently she was locked up, and was not allowed to be interviewed by any repreeentatives of the press. The prisoner is not thought to be insane, as she answered the questions put to her deliberately, and with some degree of elution. She declined to give her reasons for shooting Rossa, but it is believed she committed the act in consequence of his dynamite schemes. As soon as the woman ceased firing Rossa rose, and with assistance walked to his office, and thence to the hospital, a distance of nearly a quarter of a mile. Only one bullet pierced his body. It entered his back directly below the left shoulder blade. The wound is not considered dangerous.

The name of the woman who shot Roses (and for whose defence a subscription is mooted) is said to be really Lucilia Dudley. She is dercribed as very sensitive add rather eccen- tric. In July, 1883, she attempted suicide in a first-class carriage on the Great Eastern Railway, in England, by in- haling chloroform, and only regained consciousness after eight hours' care. While awaiting her trial she again attempted suicide, having concealed opium in the lining of her dress. She described herself as a governess and hospital nurse, and she had no relatives' and had grown despers'e through the loss of her child. She would not promise not to repeat the offencs,and in default of finding sureties went to Millbank. The chaplain brought her to a batter frame of mind, and finally assisted her to New York. She had gained excellent testimordals from Queen Charlotte's Training Hospital. A second time she attempted to poison herself on the railway, and from Lewes Gaol was sent to a lunatic asylum. Thence she seems to have gone to New York. Her prepossessing appearance and ability found her many friends. Though she described herself as a widow, it is said that she was never married. Owing to her strange behaviour and tendency to make imaginary statements, she narrowly escaped permanent detention in a lunatic asylum Only a fortnight ago the Rev. G. P. Meyrick, chaplain of Milbank, received a letter from Dudley to the effbct that

div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF
GUARDIANS,

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present— Messrs. Greening (chairman), Caldwell, Blackhurst, Darbyshire, Appleton, Forster, (iibson, Kilsball, Cooper, Brown, Grange, John Houghton Humphreys, Owen, Wm. Houghton, Bunnell, Swinton, Radcliffe, and the Rev. G. F. Roberts, J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton (assistant clerk).

THE COST OF NEWTON ELECTION. Amaccount of the expenses incurred in connection with the recent election of a Guerdian for Newton, gave the total cost of the election as £25 16e 100, of which all but £5 were for the cost of an election as fixed by the standing orders and the articles. The Clerk also beentioned that there had been five persons nottlinated for the vacancy, of whom only one pereon declined to serve. Mr. G. RadCliffe was the candidate elected. Tete MAINTENANCE OFMTINATICS.—COUNTYMATE. A letter was read from the Local Government Board in- forming the Board that they had received a communication from the Commiesioners in Lunacy in which it was sug- gested that an important proportion'of the pauper lunatics in county asylums might be adequately and more econo- mically provided for in the workhouse,—Mr. BLACKIIIIRST thought this was a step in the right direction. He was satisued from his own experience that there were a great many more people in asylums than really ought to be sent there ; they were cases that might have been treated in workhouses. That was no doubt the reason why there WAS agreet increase in the number of lunatics he the last few years.—The CHAIRMAN moved that the letter be referred to the House Committee for consideration.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE, in seconding this proposal, said he thought the medical treatment and practise the patients received at the asylum would be superior to that they would have at the workhouse, but he supposed it would he only those patients who, it Was expected would never recover that it was intended to remove to the workhouses. With reference to Mr Blackhurst's re.nark, he also pointed out that the mere removal of the patients from asylums to workhouses would not lessen the number of lunatics in the country.—Mr. JOLLEY having also supported the chairmen's proposition, it was passed.—The CLERK then explained several reductions he had made in respect of charges for the maintenance of lunatics, and slid that the statement with respect to the comity rate was less satisfactory. The amount paid on this account for the corresponding period of last year was £1,616 18s 3d, for the present half year it was £2,177 163 Id, that alone re- presenting an increase of £560 17e 10d. That showed how their Union rate worked up whttever they might do. With regard to the cost of asylums the county rate charges on the general expenditure was £473 13s, for lunatic asylums , £157 17s 7d, the county lunatic asylum loan interest ac- count was £631 10a 7d. The constabulary general expendi- ture was £B5 9u sd, for the Warringt24 division censtabu- lary £598 19s 4d, or nearly £7OO, or the police-cone stables' loan, exclusive of the Wigan division, the cost of which was issued against that Union, was £74 41 sd, amounting altogther to £700; the county wisons at Preston and larkdale £lO5 5s 21, bridges in the hundred of West Derby £5O 64 7d, total £2,177 16s Icl.—Mr4 BLACK- =Hsi' : And that all comes from what they call the poor rate P—The CLERK : Yea—Mr. DLACHEMRST : I wonder how the poor get the benefit of that ?—The CLERK : They get the name of it.

A letter was read from Messrs. W. D. Jeans and Co., solicitors, stating that they had arranged with Mr. %Verney, the solicitor of the Newton Commissioners, to postpone the expectM litigation between the Huardians and the Newton Commissioners with regard to the Harris case until the 2Gth February, the assizes being now sittine and counsel engaged at them.

THE PROPOSED ALTERATIONS AT TEE WORKHOUSE. Plans of the proposed alterations of the master's rooms by Mr. Owen, architect, were submitted. Mr. Owen also esti- mated the cost of these alterations at between no and £lOO. —Mr. BLACKHURST moved that the matter be deferred for 12 months. He aid not think this was a proper time to incur the expense, as many of the ratepayers, both farmers and tradesmen, were having hard times of it. He had no hesitation in sivinz that the cost, before everything in con- nection with the proposed alterations was completed, would probably amount to £lso.—Mr. JEANS seconded this pro- posal.—Mr. JOLLEY propssed, and Mr. APPLETON seconded, that the work be carried out at once.—After a little discus-
Mon Mr. Blickhurses motion was carried by 12 to 8

THE INDUSTRIAL SCHOOLS. " The CLERK read report of Mr. Mines the master of the Padgate Industrial Schools, as to the result of the visit of the deputation, consisting of the Chairman of the BJard, the Chairman of the School Committee (Mr. Darbyshire), Mr. Mines and the Clerk to tbe Swinton lndustriil Schools.

The report commented favourably on the mode of conducting that institution.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE mentioned that one of the objects of the deputation was to see how the children at Swinton were clothed, as some members of that Board had suggested that the children at Padgate should be more warmly clad. The deputation were, however, of opinion that their children were clothed as well as those at Swinton, I and they did not find anything to improve upon in that res- pect. Mr. Darhyshire gave a general description of what the deputation had seen, and especially commended some of the sanitary arrangements of the Swinton Schools.—Mr. CALDWELL and the CHAIRMAN having briefly rem irked on the report, the business of public interest was brought to a close.

HUTTON. • TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION.—The nsual meeting was held on Tuesday evening, at the "Layton l'ark Schools. Mr. E. f S. Eccles presided, and gave an address on the temperance principles carried out by the military expedition to the Soudan. 'loadings were contributed by Mr W D Stoba and the chairman, mad songs by Mrs Eccles, Mr H Capper, and Mr Williams. There was a good attendance. LEarunu.—On Wednesday evening a very instruotive and interesting lecture was delivered in the Ilayton Park Schoolroom, by Mrs. Hatton, of Wolverhampton, entitled 'The Nurse and the Sick 1.14)om," The rogrn watt well filled by the ldle of the neighbourhood. Mrs. Tomlinson, districi nurse, and s. few gentlemen were also present. Till Rev. Canon Penrhyn occupied the chair. Mrs. Hatton said no girl's education should be considered complvte without a course of lessons on the laws of health Having dealt with the qualification of the nurse, her relation to the medical man, to the patient, the sick room, 6.c, she concluded with practical experiments in poulice making, fomenting, and bandaging; the making of a bed for a patient, changing sheets, atm., for which purposes the plat- form had been furnished with the necessary appurtenances, and a youth acted as patient. The lecture occupied two hours, and was frequently applauded. The proceeds are to be devoted to the district nurse fund.

1101tTON LOCAL BOARD.—At the monthly meeting of the Huyton-with•Roby Local Board, on Tuesday evening, held at the Board Offices Huyton, there were present—Messrs. T. Dobell (in the chair). Siddeley, Burnyeat, Brown. Parker, Dalzell, Grimshaw, Cooper, Swift (clerk), and Dr. Hall (medical officer of health).—After the minutes of the last meeting had been•read and confirmed, a letter was read from Mr. John Jowett thanking the Board for the honour of unanimously electing him to fill the vacancy caused by the resignation of Mr. E. C. Leventon; but seeing that he was a candidate the ratepayers did not see fit to e:ect, it would not be creditable or honourable on his part to accept the position.—On the motion of Mr. Siddeley, seconded by Mr. Dalzell, it was resolved that Mr. Duncan be elected. In seconding the motion Mr. Dalzell observed that Huyton Quarry ought to be represented on the Board, and Mr. Don• can was the highest on the poll of the defetted candi- dates.

At Reading, which is to lose one member by the operation of the new reform measures, Mr. Palmer has agreed to retire, and Mr. Shaw-Lefevre, the Postmaster-General, has been accepted as the Liberal candidate. Frederick Pope, who was convicted last lession of con- spiracy in connection with certain fraudul tut public corn- panies, was brought up at the Cent* Cripainal Court on Thursday, and sentenced to five years' pen II servitude. Harry Burton, the man who was arrested by the police in Whitechapel on a charge of dealing with the trunk Cr box about which so much has been hear in connection with the explosion at the Tower, was examined before Sir J Ing- ham at Bow-street on Thursday, the charge against him be. leg that he was concerned with another man in custody in maliciously causing an explosion at the Tower an the 24th of January. The prisoner was remanded until Monday next. _ _ _
