div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 7, 1885.

SIR STAFFORD NORTHCOTE has been re- plying, after his fashion, to Mr. BRIGHT and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, Or, more particularly, to the speech of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. But he makes nothing of it; his reply is not an 'answer, and the result is an exposure of his own weakness and bad judgment in attacking an unassailable position. Be commences with a piece of sophistical misrepresentation which is not at all uncommon amongst Tory orators, though We are glad to say it is un- usual with the Devonshire baronet. He tries to make it appear that Mr. BRIGHT and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN are utterly at variance; and in order to do this he puts something into the mouth of the latter which he never said. The misrepresentation merits exposure, for we do not doubt, now that it has got on the Con- servative course, that it will be trotted out pretty often. Sir STAFFORD, speaking at Crediton, says : Mr. Barcur, as was rather his habit, had spent a good deal of Itime in a eulogium of the measures passed by Liberal Governments during the last 4o or 50 years, and the great improvements which had taken plaoe in the country; but Mr. CRIXBERLAIN had told them that, although wealth had within the last ao years increased very largely, it had done little or no good to labour generally, but that the benefit had all gone to capital. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN had spoken as if the result of the last 20 years had been to make the rich richer, and the poor poorer. Re (the speaker), however, did not think that this was quite true. But, if true what a curious commentary it was on the legislation of which Mr. BRIGHT was so proud. Assuming the Conservative leader to have correctly quoted his opponents, it must be admitted that he convicts one or other of them of being in the wrong. No objection can be taken to his reference to Mr. BIGHT'S remarks ; but every objection is to be taken to his version of the speech of Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN, who never said "the benefit had all gone to capital." What he did utter on this subject was as follows, and we invite atten- tion to it as a matter of which we shall hear something again and again : During the last zo years there has been a most extra- traordinary advance in the prosperity of this country; wealth has increased; Manulactures have developed ; invention has prospered; our exports and ink- ports have doubled and trebled. It has been calcula- ted that the annual income of the country has in- creased in this time by Goo million per annum. Well, the working classes have had some share in this prosperity. They have become more thrifty, more temperate, they are better educated, and they are, therefore, perhaps more comfortable. But their advance has not been—l think nothing is more certain—their advance has not been in propor- tion to the general average; and during the whole of this time there have been constantly in receipt of parish relief one million of perscus, or nearly one mil- lion of persons, and probably at the very least one million more have been on the verge of pauperism, During the same time 800,000 people left the land— they'have been driven or forced. to emigrate into towns.

It will be seen that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN dis- tinctly asserts that "the working classes have had some share in this prosperity " the very reverse of what Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE lays to his charge. His point is that their share has been insufficient, and that it will be his object as a politician to see that they have a better chance of better treatment in the future. Sir STAFFORD may therefore spare his jeer as to the Liberals not

NEW WORKS POE WIDNES.—The Liver Alkali Company of Liverpool have commenced the erection of their new manufactory on the Widnes and Ditton Land Company's land on Ditton-road. THE ILK:TISK CONGO COMPANY'. —ln our advertising columns to-day there will be found a prospectus of this new company, which is being established wiih a capital of £500,000 in }mow shares of £5 each. A glance at the list of directors will abow that it is receiving the counten- ance of gentlemen of sound judgment and great business capacity. There is undoubtedly a great futare in the way of trade on the Congo. Mr. H. M. Stanley has pointed out how the opening no of South-West Africa must result in im- proving the manufacturing business of Lancashire. AN OLD METHODtST.—There pissed away on Sunday one of the early promoters of Methodism. Mr. John M`Nance died at his residence, Briscoe-lane, Newton Heath. He was born at Clayton Bridge, November 10, 1805, and conse- quently had attained his 80th year. For a considerable time he had lived retired, and confined his attention solely to Sunday school work. His connection with Methodism dates back to 1821, when he joined the Wesleyan Methodist community at Culcheth Chapel. SHE DIDN'T BELIEVE WIRE DRAWERS COULD BE COM- FORTABLE—Mrs. Pugmire has a carious way of reading her paper. She first glances at all the heading, and if she finds anything that seems curious to her, makes comments on it without waiting to read the article and see if she has a clear idea of the subject. Thus she sometimes makes mis- takes, the honest old soul, which occasion her grown-up daughters much mortification. A few days ago she was looking over the paper in this way, when she saw an item headed "The Wire-Drawers," about a Strike in Pittsburg of this class of merchanics against a rabletion in their wages. " Wirmelravere ?" said the, wiping off her ei;ca: "Well, of all the ideas! What will be the next invoeation in women's dress, I wonder? Tknow that wire is made very fine, nowadays, but I don't believe they can be comfortable, and I ehould always be afraid of being struck by lightning with a pair on. Canton flannel is good enough for me in the winter time," and she moved unemily in her chair at the thought. NEWTON CONGREGATIONAL BAND OF HOPE. A very successful entertainment under the auspices of the Congre- gational Band of Hope was given in the Crow-lane Congre- gational schoolroom, on Wednesday evening. There was a very large attendance. The Rev James Allatt (pastor), who presided, said that only the other day there was buried John Rigby, who was said to be the first pledged abstainer in this country. Since he took the pledge Bands of Hope and other temperance societies had become part and parcel of nearly every Christian church in this country. During the evening the Liverpool Alexandra_ Handbell Ringers (five in number), gave several selections in a brilliant style. The proceedings were interspersed with recitations by Mr A Jones (" Dead and alone") ; Miss A Naylor t" Some- body's darling "and "Grandpa's spectacles,") -, Master J If Randall; songs by Miss Percival (" At the stile.") ; Mr W framer (" Liberty llall,") • Miss A Kitchen (" 'Twee but a dream.") ; Miss Owen (" The broken pitcher,") ; and Mr J W Caldwell (" Hurrah for the Gipsies.") Mr E Mort created considerable amusement by his rendering of the , Lancashire reading " Heaw Billy Armitage geet a neet's lodgins." A pianoforte solo by Miss E Allatt ; violin solo by Miss Glover; pianoforte duet by Messrs Corlett and A Caldwell ; and the trio "A little farm well tilled," by Messrs W Tamer, R H Jones, and J W Caldwell were also given. Miss Cameron and Mr A Caldwell efficiently ful- filled their duties as accompanists. It was recommended that the gas consumed in illuminating the public clock be charged to the public clock amount, and that a separate meter be attached. It was oleo recommended that the two windows at the east end of market hall be altered by adding to the loottom extra lights of transparent glass and -stall boards, so that goods exhibited for sale may be seen from the outside. It was recommended that the following scale of payments to the fire brigade be adopted in lieu of the rates now in force, the alteration to take effect on April Ist, 1885:—Remuneration for attendance at dr.ll—Super- intendent, £0 per annum; deputy-superintendent, £3 103; firemen (each), £2 108; call boys (each), Ll 104. Re- muneration for attendance at fires—Superintendent, 3s first hour, and is GI every succeeding hour; firemen (each), 2s ditto, and Is ditto; and helpers, 9d per hour.— Mr Debson, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the members would be surprised to see that the receipts at the I market were being reduced. He was only appointed chair- man of the committee last month, but be had ascertained that dating the past 44 weeks there bad been received from the shops £39 3e, whilst for the corresponding period in 1883 the amount was £53 Is 3d, a decrease of £l4 18s 3d. ' The income from the large mach:— for a similar period in 1883 was £4B 83 93, last year £33 10a 91, decrease £l4 Its. . The receipts from the small machine showed a decrease of 31. The tolls received on the market and fair ground amounted during 44 weeks in 1883 to £164 43 3d, last year £l6O 2e 21, de- crease £4 24 Id, whilst there was also a decrease of 16s per month in the amount received from the hawkers. The de- crease in the amount received from the weighing machine was explained by the fact that Messrs Wigg Bros. and Steele had erected one of their own. He explained that last quarter there was an increase of £7 in the bill for gas at the Market Hall, and in consequence it was deckled to have a separate meter for the clock. SELLING BUTTERINE AS BUTTER : HEAVY PENALTIES.— Before Messrs F. W. Earle and W. Pilkington, at the Pres- cot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, John Trueedale, of the Derby Stores, Eccleston-street, Prescot, was summoned for an offence under the Adulteration of Food and Drugs Act, by selling as butter an article known as butterine.—P.C. Stirzeker, stationed at Huyton, s'ated that on the 16th Janu- ary be visited several shops in Prescot, under the directions of Superintendent Barker, to purchase a number of samples of butter for the purpose of analysis. Amoeg other places, he called at defendant's shop and asked for a pound of shilling butter. He was supplied by the defendaat, who, on being told it was for analysis, said it was always wrapped in a paper on which was a labePthat it was butterine. The certificate received from the analyst stated that the sample contained 11 3-sths per cent of water and 71 per cent of fresh fats.—The defendant urged that he did not know he was offending against the law, and remarked that he always wrapped the butterine in paper, upon which it was stated that it was butterine.—The Bench considered the case a very bad one and inflicted a tine of £4 and costs.--James Johnston, grocer, Kemble-street, was summoned (era similar offence.—Mr. Mackenzie, solicitor, Prescot, appeared for the defendant.—ln this case P.C. Strirzaker asked for a pound of shilling butter, and the defendant replied I have not got any shilling butter, but I have some at 101" He pur- chased a pound at 10d, and on the defendant being told that it was for analysis he pointed to a printed label, giving the price, and beneath which, in small letters, was the word " butterine." The analysis of the sample showed that it contained 8 per cent of water and 72 per cent of fresh fats. —Mr. Mackenzie maintained that the article was not sold to the prejudice ,of the buyer, and urged that the buyer had been supplied with an article for which he asked.—Tbe Bench decided to inflict a similar fine as in the last case, nam ly, £4 and costs.—Ann Benson, who keeps a grocer'a shop in Kemble-street, was also summoned for a like offence. The sample purchased by the constable contained 10 per cent of water and 70 per cent of fresh fats.—The defendant pro- duced the ticket on which the price was marked, and beneath In small letters was the word " butterine." She stated that those who asked for shilling butter knew what it was.—The Chairman said the Bench are determined to preeect the pub. lic, and not only the public, but the poor people who eat this nasty stuff. They are of opinion that you must be con- victed in the same way as the others, and must pay a fine of £1 and Costs.

The amount received from outside stalls in 1879 80 was £152 58 41; in 1882-83, £l7l Os 7d; increase, £2O; and last year, 1883-84, the amount received I was £lB7 6s 61, an increase of £35 over 1880. To his mind this indicated that they had transferred these receipts from the inside of the market to the outside. He thought this was brought about by the fact that the Board constructed stalls of a very substantial and convenient character, and the consequence was that people who formerly occupied Chops in the inside of the market took those stalls and went forward into the street. He opposed the proposal of the committee to construct windows at the east end of the market, on the ground that they would compete unfairly with the tradesmen in the town; and pointed out that the decrease from 1880 to 1883-84 was only £24—from .£342 to £3lB—so that there was really nothing very alarming. He moved that the minutes be referred back. Mr. Norman seconded. In reply to Mr. Dobson, the Surveyor said it was esti- mated that each window would cost £5.
The Chairman thought it would be r; great mistake to ex- pend any money on this experiment. Mr. Lightburn supported the amendment, which was carried.
The minutes as amended were then adopted. FINANCE.

showed that there were 38 honorary and 63 active and associate members. The report closed by a reference to the treat to the aged people, which they now believed was fairly established amongst the permanent institutions of the town. (Applause) Mr. J. E Meredeth, the treasurer, read his report, which showed that there was a small deficit on the year's working. The Chairman delivered a brief address, in which be dealt With the report, and remarked that the association did not do the amount of evangelical work it ought to do. He ap- °proved of the attempts to form a gymnasium, and suggested that the members should consider the advisability of ob- taining a small field which had been pointed out to him as suitable for croquet, lawn tennis, eke. lie failed to find in the Free Library reading-room any of those who had been in the habit of attending the association. He hoped no young man would think it right to give up his membership to go down to the Free Library in order that he might get his literature free. (hear, hear.) Several times during the past year he had been pained to see so few young men in the Aso elation rooms, and he thought, considering the advantages offered to members, there ought to he a better attendance. He urged the members to endeavour to increase the member- ship. Referring to the aged persons treat, the Chairman said he hoped, and he thought every member hoped, that this treat would be continued every year. (Applause.) On the motion of Mr. J. K. Digges, seconded by Captain Le Coutier, the report was adopted. In eulogistic terms Mr. Coventry moved, and Mr. W. Shaw seconded, and Mr. J. K. Digges supported a cordial vote of thanks to Mr. Beckett for his services as president. —lt was carried by acclamation, and the President replied. —Mr. Coventry proposed that Mr. John Johnson be sp. ^ pointed president for the ensuing year, but Mr. J declined the honour.—lt was then unaeimously decided Oa the prop )sition of Mr. Coventry, seconded by lve. G. Howard, that Mr. T. Norman be aeked to accept the office. The hearty thanks of the meeting were accorded to the treasurer, and the secretaries, and Messrs. Meredith, W. Pownall, jUll, and S. H. Dawson replied in suitable terms. These officers were also unanimously re-elected. The fol- lowing were constituted members of the clmrnittee :-Messrs. W. Shaw, C. Nickson, T. Cooke' S. Covervry, C. A. Dew- eon, W. IL Rogerson, G. Howard, and J. E. Longshaw.—On the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. W. Pownall, Jun., the thanks of the meeting were accorded to the vice- president, the committee, the Rev. T. Arnascn (chairman of the bible class), and Mr. C. Nickson (secretary of the his.tirical . proceedings then terminated. THE RUNC DRN GAS WORKS BILL.—TIIE COMMISSIONERS DEFEATED. On Teursday evening, a ratepayers' meeting, convened by the Board of Commissioners, was held in Bethesda Schoolroom, to approve and give consent to the opposing by the Commissioners of a Bill now pending in Parliament to enable the Rancotn Gas Company to raise additional capi- tal, construct new works, &e., and to Banc ion the ap,.ly iag of the public fonds or rates under the control of the Com- missioners to the payment of the costs and expenses atten- ding such opposition. Mr. Robert Shaw presided. Mr. LIGHTBIIIIN, in moving a resolution in ac:mdance with the purpose stated above, said that the Company pro- posed to extend their operations, and were seeking power to raise new funds to the amount of £20.000. There was a standard price of gas of 3s. 41. per thousand cubic feet, and a sliding scale fixed, which provided that for every penny added to the standard price of gas there should be a quarter per cent deducted from the interest, and for every penny taken from Dv standard price the interest could be increased by a quarter per cent. The Commissioners thought this standard price ought to be reduced to 35., the price the con- sumers actually paid for gas. The ratepayers might depend that the board would not go to Pa: I iameut without ex- hausting all other means of coming to an amicable con- clusion. (Applause.)

, Mr MEADowcaorr seconded the motion. Mr. W. HAYES said that they in Runcorn knew how much they had suffered by going to law, and he wanted to persuade them not to go to Parliament to op- pose this bill. The Company did not want to make extor- tionate charges. Mr. F. RIGBY said the policy of the Company had not been to otain as much money as thy could in the way of dividend, but to supply at a fair and equitable price gas of good quality to its consumers. He said that the policy of chargiag low rates had been an infallible test of the Com- psny's honesty. (Applause.) The Company had promoted this bill with the greatest reluctance. He was certain that the endeavour of the Company would be not to sell gas at 3s 6d, but as much lower as they could, and to deal with them as they had done, in a liberal and honest spirit. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Lion'rnrrnN said if the Commissioners founl that they were asking for that which was not fair and reasonable they would not oppose the Bill. Mr. ADAMS said that if they caused the Gas Company to spend £l,OOO in promoting their Bill the consumers would have to pay for it in the future. (Hear, hear.) Mr. H. Cots/3ERN asked the ratepayers to leave the matter in the hands ef the Gas Company. The CHAIRMAN observed that at the present time the Runcorn Gas Company, charging 35 2d for gas, with a dis- count of 21, were enabled to pay the shareholders 10 per cent dividend, and the Commissioners, under these circum- stances wished to know why they asked for a standard price of 3s 6J. Considering that the Company could pay a I good dividend, and charge 3s per 1,000 feet, he thought that the Board was not asking anything unreasonable when they sariamseurkn°Ltitn., and to desmirre.dßthwerisytansadial standard to bet afinxdeadr da t the o.f3s oppose the Bill in the hope of getting such a standard would be throwing money away. Mr. Meadowcroft considered 10 per cent, a handsome dividend, and asked why should the company not give the ratepayers the benefit of all they made over that per cen- tags. He thought the Gas Company could afford to fix the sliding scale at 3s. (Applause.) The resolution was then Out and lost by a large majority.. _ _ _
Mr. Rigby moved, and Dr. McDougall seconded, a vote of thanks to the chairman, and the motion was carried unani- mously.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Present: Lieutenant-Col. Ashton (in the chair), the Revs J W N Tanner, J Lockwood, Messrs Norman, 11 Ashton, Weir, Aaron, Wallingt in, Speakman, Mclntyre, Handley, Rigby, W Whitlow, Lowe, Hamilton, Wallington, Knowles, Smith, Stokes, Canykin, Actois,U Linaker (clerk), I and W H Linaker (deputy clbrk). ; Tirr. WESTON PAY OFFICE.— Mr Aaron moved that the relieving of-fleet's pay station at Weston be dispensed with. He contended that under the present arrangement the per. sne in receipt of out-door relief were not properly attended to —ln answer to qu-stions, it was stated that them o were nine paupers at Weston, and the pay station cast 10e. per year.—Mr Acton seconded the motion. —Mr Handley pointed out that a pay office was a great convenience, but the present office was only just beyond the bt undaries of Runcorn, and he proposed as an amendment that Mr Wright In his discretion, give notice of the termination of the tenancy of the present place, and engage another office nearer the centre of the district.—Mr Norman seconded the amendment, which was carried by nine votes to eight. THE VAGRANCY DIFFICULTY laiD SroNsmausuirici.—The Deputy Clerk read letters that had been received from vari- ous Unions as to the cost of erecting vagrant wards for stonebreaking. It appeared that at Knutsford they were , erected at a cost of £550 ; at Nantwich on the separate cell I system eight cost £OOO (loud laughter) ; at Warrington ten separate wards for £500; at Northwich nine on the separate cell system for £6OO ; and at Macclesfield 16 sep- arate cells were built of wood for about £6o.—Mr. P. Speak- , man : That would suit us.—Mr. Rigby : That is too much ; by one-half.—At Preto n Union 22 Cells for etonebreaking were erected for £5OO, and at Tarvin the system had not been adopted.—Mr. Rigby remarked that they were sensible people.—Mr. Speakman moved, and Mr. Smith seconded, that the letters be referred to the Visiting C, mmittea for consideration.—Tne Rev. J. Lockwood thought the Board I ought to really avoid anything that was unnecessary-(hear, I hear)—at this time, when there was such a depression in trade (Hear, hear.) He thereupon moved that the matter Ibe not referred to the committee.-Mr. Rigby, Mr. Hamilton, I aid Mr. Aaron all rose to second the gmendmeot. Mr. Aaron said they could carry on stonebreaking without wards. He suggested that each vagrant should be I given two cwt to break before break ast.—Mr. Rigby : That is not the question, Aaron. (Laughter.) Mr. Mclntyre ' hoped the matter would be considered in the interests of ' economy to keep tramps from the Union.—The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner: In the depression of the agricultural interest I ' think we should be wrong indeed to do aoythinz of the ' kind. I protest against it.—Mr. St)eakinan suggested that the clerk should inquire from other Unions what had been the result and the cost of stone-breaking.—Mr. Rigby: We ,• shall want another clerk directly, I can see. (Laughter.)— ; The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner: I protest against it being enter- tained at all.—Mr. Speakman contended that stone-breaking would be a benefit to the house.—The Clerk pointed out ih a Mr. Speakman's motion was unnecessary, as the Visiting Committee had already power to consider the question, and the Rev. J. Lockwood therefore moved that it be an instruc- tion to the committee not to proceed any further with the matter.—Mr. Hamilton seoonded.—Mr. W. Handley said that from the letters read it appeared that the Unions on every side of theru had adopted the stone-breaking test, and the consequence would be that in order to avoid the stone- breaking the vagrants would dock to the Runcorn Union, and they would not be able to accommodate them in the I house. He would not go into any elaborate expenditure, because he had very great sympathy with the views ex- pressed lsv Mr. Lockwood rnd Mr. Tanner, but he thought they could adopt the stone-breaking test without any ex- pense beyond about £5. ;Meer, hear.) They had on the premises men who bad rut op in a -substantial and work- 'manlike manner two or three buildings which might be called pernaanent, and bo suggested that an open shed with a roof of corrugated iron would meet all requirements. Opium picking was very unremunerative, and he was car- tam 'slat the stone-breaiking test would be a great advan- tage.—The Rev. J. Lockwood thought tire stone-breaking 'system a good one; he believed in the principle of the thing.—After a little further discussion, Mr. Lockwood's tauten was carried.—Mr. Whitlow then moved that Mr. Jones in his own discretion introdnce the stone-breaking eystem out of doom, and without the expense of erecting abets or wards.—Mr. Speakman said he had simply brought forward the matter in the interests of the Union. They would have to come to the system sooner or later.—The Clerk quoted some figures showing the increase in vagrants in the Union, and Mr. Handley bold that it was because the:stone-breaking tett was in force in the surrounding Uniens.—Mr. Jones was called into the room, and stated that there were no facilities about the house for stone- breakng. The vagrants could not be left alone in the yard. They would abscond over the wall. (Laughter.)— Mclntyre : I would leave the wall tow so that they could get awty.—Mr. Jones added that when vagrants bad only to stay one night there WAS only a third of the number them were now.. Formerly there were only nine or ten a week ; now there were from 20 to 30. They went there for a day's rest. —The Chairman: Do you tell the Board that it is im- possible to adopt the test of stone-breaking.—Mr. Jones : Unless you make provision for it. You cannot put them in an open yard without them absconding.—Mr. Rigby : Let them abscond. They will only have had one supper and breakfast.—Mr. Handley explained that according to the Casual Poor Act 1882 vagrants had to stay in the house two nights and one day.—Eventually it was decided that the Visiting Committee Eh ould consider the best way of dealing with the vagrants.
RUNCORN YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIA- TION.

The annual meeting of the members of this association was held in the rooms, High-street, and there was a good attendance. Tea, provided by Mr Mona, of the Cocoa Rooms, having been partaken of, Mr S C Beckett took the chair. Amongst those present were the Rev T M Armson, Captain Le Coutier, Messrs W Shaw, S Coventry, F J Nor- man, G Howard, T Cooke, J Smith, H Fitton, J John- son, A C Dawson, Hankinson, .1 E Meredith, W Po snail (hon sec), and S H Dawson (assistant sec). The Hon Secretary read the annual report which stated that the year from a financial point of view, had been a very successful one, and the president who had thrown himself heartily into all the undertakings of the committee, was highly complimented. The year opened with a balance of £9 7s Bd, which enabled the committee to undertake some evangelical work, w..ich for several years owing to the lack of fail& they had been unable to engage in. A week's ser- vices were therefore conducted by Mr Hefford, of the Evan- gelical Society, the nett cost being £3 18s lid. The com- mittee believed a fortaight's services might be held, and trusted to have- the hearty co-operation of the members. During the year attempts had been made in conjunction with the Football Club to establish a gymnasium in con- nection with the association, but, after thoughtfully going into the various schemes suggested, and inspecting several sites and buildings, the committee were most reluctantly compelled to abandon the idea for the prestnt. They, how- ever, recommended the establishment of a fund to be called "The Gymnasium Fund," and to again bring forward the subject, when sufficient money was raised to afford reasonable hope of success. The work of the Histolical Society and the Bible Class was briefly reviewed, and refer- ence was made to the annuli soiree in May, the plc-nic held in July, and to the provision of the smoke-room and bagatelle table. The reading-room still continued to be fairly well patronised, although the committee had to con- tend against the four reading-rooms where similar advan- tages were offered. Thanks were offered to all those who had given pipers and books during the year. The roll-book

BILLY BIND'S KESSUNIN.

The 4th of July dawned upon the sleeping hamlets vs,lth a cheerful sun, that as the day throve apace increased in vigour until at noon its rays poured with a fierce intensity upon the spires and vanes of the church and the roofs of the rose-covered cottages. The atmoThere was sultry heyond endurance, the scent of the perfume...laden zephyr alone disturbed it, and intimated to the hot and dusty way- farer that Nature was not asleep. Save for the passing breeze everything seemed to enjoy an endless siesta, The cottage doors were tenantless, the bees forsook their pollen- gathering, and sought the shelter of their hives, while the dogs winked lazily from their half-shut eyes, in sheer inability to bark. The stillness of the Sabbath afternoon was abruptly broken by the sharp, intermittent tolling of "tin' ovvd church 'bell. As the monotonous banging fell upon the ear, proclaiming the hour of baptism, a couple might have been seen slowly wending their way thereunto. The man, being ne superior animal, walked first, and as he raised his "shiner" to mop his heated brow with a large striped belcher handkerchief, he disclosed the features of Billy Brid. The partner of his joys and sorrows toiled wearily after him, bearing in her arms a huge bundle that alnfost defied detection as to its contents, if judged from the shape. A sudden scream, however, betrayed the secret. Billy turned on hearing the sound, qnd hastily demanded Wod's up ?" "Aw dorn'd know," returned Melly, his batter-half, "happen id's hongry. Here, tek this bag un ged one eaut." Billy thus addressed took the bag, Out whether the continued shrieking of the infant made him nervous or petulance was the cause, the snap he made at the aforesaid bag left him wit; a piece of paper in his hand, while the biscuits Were scattered in varied directions. The next five minutes were spent by Billy in inwardly con- signing "th' biscuits" to another and more distant locality, after which he carefully wrapped them up in his " hanker- cher.* Then .the trio proceeded onwards. By this time they had reached the church door, where Billy was met by "th' dark," who received a deferential nod and a look of awe from both parties. In reply to Billy's whispered interrogatioraV•th' clark" said "tin' pa'son hedn'd come. Wohla they step forrud." Ac- cordingly, having deposited his umbrella and hat on a secluded seat, Billy and" th' wifs " stole up the chancel on tiptoe and sat near the font. After waiting some minutes for the minister Billy's natural restlessness asserted itself. " Aw'm dry, Mally," he said at last, "Sit theer, an' am% slip reaund to th' Mitre." " Theau'll do no sich thing," said • Mally, rising, If theau wants to sup thad bad, there's plenty o' watter thad theer " (pointing to the font). Billy rose, placed his hand oveathe edge, and not touching any- thing wet, clambered upon the side of the font, resting his stomach on the edge. Just then a sudden cry from the infant caned him to lose his balance, and amid a variety of fantastic evolutions, in which a pair of struggling legs were the principal feature, cllled loudly for help. Mally deposited the child on the cashioa, and seizing her liege lord by the legs, pulled him out of the basin, and deposited him on the Boor. Just then the minister walked leisurely up thvaisle. Billy instantly jerked his handkerchief out ef his pocket, forgetting the biscuits. The cracking they made upon the tessalated floor brought a crimson flush to his face, and he 'wished fervently "th' greannel nd oppen, an swallow him up." The minister now took the infant in his arms and Billy waited for " th' manifestations." Turning to our, friend, " th' pa'son " inquired, " What's your name ? "id's nod me as wants keentn," said Billy, "id's the youngster." '"You are irreverent, young I man," said the minister. "Nay aw'ra nod," said Billy, " aw'm a weyver." The priest started perceptibly, but pro- ceeded to read the formula for baptism. Billy repeated the clerk's words, or rather re-echoed them in a tolerably correct manner, occasionally replying with the startling reply, "I announce them .111." At length the Question came, "What is the name of this child ?!' Billy reddened, as he replied slowly, "Brid." "Is that his Christian name?" inquired the priest. "Neaw," said Billy, "he hez il o' th' year round. Id's nod his liesrous name." "What ii his ear- name?" " Wod dun yo mean?" said Billy. "His second name, his appellation." "Ave dorn'd understand you, bud his front name's Billy, same as mine," returned the some- what confused father. The infant was invested with its cognornen, the minister wisely referring to the feminine parent, as being rather more au fait than her lord and mas- ter. The child being duly christened, and Mr. Brid having affixed the sign of multiplication to an official register, they proceeded home, Billy emphatically declaring that "Besunt or nod kesunt, he'd be smoort if he went theer on thad errand again." What our friend's embarrassment and perplexity would have been had he officiated as the parent of a dual offspring, it is impossible to even surmise.

On &attar Jay evening a presentation was alere on behalf of tho past and present students-of Warrington School of Art to Mr. Thompson, the head-master, on his retirement„.l after balding that position for nearly 30 years. It was also partizioated in by other friends of Mr. Thompson. The token of goodwill took the shape of a portrait in oil, and the ceremony of presenting it took plane at the Lion Hotel, Leing preceded by an excellent dinner provided by the manageress, to which about, thirty gentlemen sat down. The chair was occupied by Mr. Thomas Morris, and the vice-chair by Councillor Wright. Amongst those also pie- sent were Aldermen Pickmere and Webster, Councillors Roberts, Dr. Mackie,T. Sutton,.W. Bolton, and Messrs Thos. Dirties, F. Monks, J. L. Whittle, Price, J. L. Tunstall, W. Perry, J. Hesketh, C. Twiss, W. Owen, W. Read, J. Pater- son, Pendlebnry, Pilkingtoo, Young, W. Fell, W. Roberts, (architect, Manchester,) Bentley (School of Art, Birken- head), J. Green (solicitor,,Manchester), &-c.—On the concha. sion of the repast the usual loyal patriotic touts were given from the chair and duly honoured.

Responding to the "Army, Navy, and Reserve Forces." I with which his name was coupled, A'derman TICIMEHE I said that at the present time we were all interested in the English Army and what it was doing in Egypt. (Hear, hear.) All would have read of the success which that little band of intrepid men had bad in their toilsome march from , Korti to Gakdal, and then to Metemmeh. It was a wonder.- I ful thing, and would redound to the credit cf England for 1 many years. • Re thought that all military critics would say that but for taeir pluck, energy, and peraevprancw that little band of hsroes could not have escapod death. (Ap- plause.) Mr. WHITTUR then read letters from gentlemen who were not able to attestd the gathering. Mr. IA Smith, writing as a friend and fellow-student of Mr. Thompson, from Brad- ford Technical College, saiil that he should have enjoyed participating in the well-earned tribute to Mr. Thompson's character and professionalcareer which.thepresentation of his portrait implied. Had he been present be should have felt obliged, it seemed to him, to say something for the men who had borne the burden and heat of the day in the field

of art edpcation. Those who lead seen the unfo'ding of the scroll of tuitional history, from the hemiliation in /851 to the comparative triumph of 1885, knew very well to whom belonged the credieof thia change, and on whom had fallen the task of bringing, it about. Not by national action, but in spite of its inertness and discouragements, not by the nurture Of local manufactures from central authorities, but , through the patient work of a handful of art missionaries labouring beetles provinces (which bad been invariably snubbed and neglected by the central department) had Ibis national work, of progress in industrial art education been achieved. It was, therefore, only a fitting and deserved recognition which- Mr. Thompsotee pupils made, that the image of their master, who wee the his- torical pioneer of art eduction in Warringten, should remain with them as a memorial and a testimoay. Mr John Itylands wrote expresing pleasure at being able to subscribe to the presentation, and Mr Henry Woods, writ- ing from Venice, to Mr Birtles, regretted that be could not , be present. The Ceternmeee said that the opinions these letters ex- pressed could not be more sincere than was his own, and his heart beat as warmly towards Mr Thompson, though he was a new friend, as it did to his oldest friend in Warring- ton. When the old students apperled to him to assist in doing homage to whom homage. was due, he did so with his whole heart, for he felt that Mr Thompson hid worked up the School of Art to its present position. He ha I, toe, in- spired eome of his Old etudents b 7 his zeal, and when they 1 bad left bins they e'eone as stars in the world of art. This I mast be due to a teacher who loved his work, for unless a I teacher loved his work his students could not gain that !success they would otherwise attain. They could not in any case feel the same warm-heartedness as when they had a teacher like Mr Thompson. No man, he believed, had worked so bard tewards the building of the new School of Art as had Mr Thompson, and he, if anyone did, dew- ! ved a laurel. (Hear, bear.) He knew they would be proud i to join him in saying that our School of Art was second to i none in the kingdom. He then called upon Mr Birtles to present the portrait to Mr Thompson. (Applause.)—Three cheers having been given to Mr and Mrs Thompson, Mr BIRTLES rose to mike the presentation. It was, he remarked, nearly 30 years since thee first met Mr Thompson, in the days of the old School of Art. He was the first, or nearly so, to meet Mr. Thompson, and was about the first who was brought into feememeee contact with him. That was 29 years ago, and I from then e bond of friendship had been established i between himself till 6" elfand Mr. Thempeen. (Aleelause ) wh'r i Mr. Thompson took possession of the school, the energy I and dermination he infused into his work encouraged his I peelle and established the fmndatien of the success that I had been abed by Warritlgtee students. A good master I made good pupils, atid the etudents fiellet to Fedi lletitte Mr. I Thompson with a determination that they would achieve 1 something worthy of them, and he need scarcely mention that to-day there were students who had gone front that school of whom they as Warringtonians had all reason to Ibe proud. There were some of them who, he believed, would attain the highest summit of success in art in Eng- land if God gave strength to work. That was saying a I deal fer the School of Art, and if it had only accomplished 1 that it had accomplished much. That presentation was not a monum set erected to Mr. Thompson. The monument ' erected to him in eilusermiltreet would live in ages to come, I when, perhaps, the portrait had perished. They bad reason to thank Mr. Thompson for the energy, determine- ! lion, and pluck that had ctraractised his art cireer in War- rington. Ile then asked Mr. Thompson's acceptance of the ; portrait. (Applause.) He had an additional duty to dis- charge. When the presentation to Mr. Thompson was I being considered, he in a casual way mentioned it to Mr. ' Shetfield—(cbeers)—who immediately offered to give them a picture. The result was before them in the shape of a beautiful black and white sketch. He thought they would all awes that it was work well worthy of Mr. Sheffield, whose name was celebrated throughout the world as a pro- ducer of black and white sketches. Mr. Birtles concluded by making the seccnd presentation. (Applause.) Mr. Tnompeoer was greeted with cheers on rising to reply. He felt sincerely and deeply the honour paid him, and regretted that he cmild not sufficiently thank them for such consideration, gocti opinion, and manifest proof of , their kind feelings towards him as was evidenced by the I presentation of that testimonial. It waa a proof of their I esteem arid respect on his retirement, and he accepted the I offering with more pride than he could express. They would be as pleased as he was to learn that the portrait would fihd its home in the Art Gallery—(applause)—that it had graciously been accepted by their friend,. Mr. , Beamont, the chairman of the Museum and Art Gallery ' Committee. When be was reminded that that was the third token of their kind feeling his difficulty was increased, and he could scarcely find words in which to express his feelings. It was very pleasing to receive the testimonials from the hands of his old friend,. Mr. Slalom That gentle- man was on of hie oldest pupilsrand he did not know how he could better receive them than from him. Mr. Sheffield. was pleased to execute that work, So full of power and skill, at his (Mr. 'Thompson's) own house, in the presence of many now present, a few weeks ago, as a memento of his friendship and kind feelings. He regretted that Mr. Sheffield was not present to receive his sincere acknowledgment of that valu- able gift. Every. artist would admit that it was a masterpiece—and it was commenced and finished in lees- than two hours and a half. (Applause.) His long connec• lion with the Schools of Art, the good will and kindness at all times evidenced by his students and his friends,. would ever remain green in his memory. (Loud applause) Alderman WEBSTER, who was next called on, said be thought that the Museum Committee would have great pleasure in receiving the portreit, and that there must be something gratifying and pleasing to Mr. Thompson and the other gentlemen who were engaged in teaching art or in the furtherance of art principles, in that presentation, which was an encouragement to them to press forward in their work. In a school, pupils required to feel that they were progressing, and if a teacher could make his pupils not only love him, but their work also, it was a great point gained, , and one of the surest ways of procuring success in art. He thought, from along connection with Warrington Scbool of Art, he might say that the efforts of Mr. Thompson had been of an admirable character. Their thanks were due te him for his _energy in promoting the success of the school.— Mr. BENTLEY, master of Birkenhead School of Art, ex- pressed pleasure at his being present.—Dr. Memel; in a. speech of considerable length, proposed "Success to the School of Art.' f It was a proposal that meant the burying of hatchets and a prolonging of the deep interest in the School of Art which Warrington people had evinced for an entire generation. Mr. Thompson ho had known since ho came to Warrington, and the school he had known from its I infancy. He coupled the name of Mr. Owen with the toast. , —Responding, Mr. OWEN Baia that to him, as secretary, the , Schools of Art was of considerable iaterest. lehad so far been successful, through the exertions of the committee and of MaThompson,and he was satisteed that the success would continue. It was, he mentioned, through Mr. 'Thompson ' that Mr Crosfield—whoee name they could not mention without great respect—offered them the Sum Of £l,OOO. (Applause.) Ile hoped all would put their shoulders to the wheel and make the school still more successful—The Vrez-Cneweeten read a letter from Mr Middleton, Halifax. _ . ..

expressing his sympathy with the occasion, and his con- gratulations to Mr Thompson. fle then proposed "The Visitors," csupling with it the names of Messrs Sutton, Roberts, and Green, who suitably acknowledged the com- pliment.—Mr BIRTLES proposed the health of Alderman Webster and Mr Felt, which were cordially honoured and responded to.—Alderman PICILMERE proposed "Town and Trade," to which Mr Monks responded, and the health of the Chairman was proposed by Mr ROBEBTS.—In propos- ing the healths of the "Old Boys" and students generally Mr TuouPsott said that the high position of the School of Art was as much due to the industry and willingness of the students to at all times help on the work, a 3 it was to him- self. He wished to thank Mr Crosfielet for his noble gift of £l,OOO towards the new School, and being the means of giving to the town a good and suitahlabome for the work of the school, so long wanted and so much needed. He must also thank the subscribers to the fund towards the building and the ladies who formed themselves into a committee and gave their services to obtain the amount necessary to complete the building. He hoped that the time would come when the school might be taken over hy the Corporation without interfering with the mnsenin rate,
and believed it wne.Mr Crosfield's feeling that the C:arporation should take the building.—Daring the evening several songs were sang,. Mr F S Peudlebary acting as- acme. panist. . .

The portrait presented to Mr. Thompson is the work of Mr. Herbert Johneton, of Manchester, and is a capital like- ness. It is half-length style, and depicts Mr. Thompson, who is wearing a light overcoat loosely thrown book, stand- ing with a port-crayon in his hand, as though he might. have just entered the School of Art and was contemplating , a picture. It is a vigorous painting, and undoubtedly one lof Mr. Johnston!s best productions The frame is rich and of handsome design, and an inscription suitably sets forth the fact that the picture was made the subject of a presen- I tation to Mr. Thompson. The drawing by Mr, _Sheffield is I a black and white marine sketch, disclosing two fiShi2g I smacks in a rough se3,and is one such as only Mr. She ffiAa could produce._

div.p: EARLESTOWN.

Tairrsraa.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, ort Saturday, Mr. Richard Lythgoe applied for the transfer to him of the license of the Prince of Wales Hotel, Earle- street, Earlestown, now held by his father, :cseph Lytbgoe. —The Bench granted the application. ENTILITAMIENT. —There was a large attendance at a public entertainment given in the Good Templars Lodge Room, Bridge-street, on Saturday evening. The chair was occupied by Brother George E. Warburton, and a capital programme of part songs, duets, solos, readings, and reci- tations was creditably gone through. A. pleasant evening I was spent.

CHAERL CHOIR SOCIAL GATHERING The members of the choir and a few friends connected, with the Primitive Methodist Chapel, .Legh-street, Earlestown, held their annual social gathering on Wednesday evening. An excel- lent tea was partaken of in the schoolroom ; the two tables being presided over by ladies of the oongregation. After tea the party, numbering about 40, spent the evening in an enjoyable manner under the presidency of the Rev F N Sbimmin (resident minister). ' Several games, dth, were in- terspersed with selections of music by members of the choir.

Sr. MARY'S CATHOLIC SCHOOL, CROW LANE —St. Mary's Catholic School, Crow-lane, Newton was well filled on Monday evening, when the school girls gave a representa- tion of the attric•ive drama, "The Chinese Mother." The girls had undergone a careful training at the hands of Miss Torpey, the schoolmistress, and the manner in which the piece was performed reflected the highest credit upon that lady, as well as upon those who sustained the various characters. The dresses were beautiful, and not a hitch , occurred. The prineipal parts were sustained as follow "The Rev. Mother of the Sisters of Charity at Hong Kong," Miss Mary Toole; "Sister Margaret," Mice Mary A. Loftus; " Apiou " (a Chinese lady), Miss Monica Hughes; "Shuey Ping Sin ' (a confidential servant of a mandarin), Miss Mary H. Touhey ; "Saau-Mel " (a Chinese widow), Miss Margaret Ronayne; Assom" (Chinese boatman's wife, Miss Elizabeth A. Gordon ; "Chinese Fondlings," Misses Mary Dee, Mary A Rice, and Teresa Colquit ' • and " Biddy IVPGrath " (an Irish widow), Miss Mary Bartley. During the performance, Miss Riley, of Earlestown, sang with ex- cellent effeat "Killarney's Lakes," and was rewarded with prolonged applause. A GROCER'S AccorrNr.—At Warrington County Court on IThursday, before his honour Judge Ffoulkes, Thomas Chubb, Burtonwood, was summoned by Simon Hazleton, provision dealer, Burtenwood, for the payment of £d 13s 61d owing for goods delivered.—Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the plaintiff.—lt appeared that the defendant and his wife had been separated, and the goods had been supplied before they were separated. They were, since that time, living to- gether again.—Defendant, who appeared in person. said be knew nothing of the bill, and plaintiff should have let him know his wife was having the goods.—Mrs. Chubb had been subpcened to give evidence in the case, but did not appear. —His Honour said that a woman bad no authority to pledge her husband's credit, unless she was put to the necessity of doing it. If a man supplied his wife with sufficient money for their needs the inference was that the wife had no au- thority to take his credit. In thia Case the husband had apparently ample means, and there was no reason why he should not pay for things as he got them. He swore that he did not owe a penny, and the fact that he repudiated the account as soon as he received ic was consistent with his story that he supplied his wife with sufficient money, and never contemplated her getting thins 911 entlit hits name. Jadgment Weatiel De for o_efendant, with costs. TEE TALE OF A GoAT.—Richard Davison, a resident of the Vulcan, was summoned at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Messrs. George McCorquodale, T. J. Gillespie, C. Pilkington, A. C. McCorquodale, and W. F. Gooch, for assaulting a lad named Frederick Mee, Mr. Browne, solicitor, Warrington, appeard for the cam- plaigent, and 0210er:relent pleaded not guilty —From the statement of Mr. Brovin; !a,wreared thgt the eamplsinant was the nephew of Mr. Charles Pennington, farmer, Newton. The latter had a goat, which unfertunately got lost some weeks ago, but he subsequently heard that it Ives in the possession of the defendant. He thereupon sent his nenhew, the complainant, alone with another boy named Braddock to get the goat and bring it home. The lads went to defen- dants house at the Vulcan, and saw Mrs. Davison, who gave them the goat. They were bringing it away, and had got as far as Wargraye Church, when the defendant came after them and overtook them. He asked what they were doing with the goat, and the complainant replied, "Oh, it's ours, and I'm taking it home. If there is anything to pay for it my uncle will pay." The defendant then told the lads to catch the goat and' return it to him, but they refused to do 50, whereupon he s-ized the complainant by the coat collar and pushed him into the hedge. The defendant himself afterwards tried to catch the goat, and on failing again seized the complainant and held him until the goat came up. The defendant thereupon caught it and took it back to his hoisee.---Evidence to support of Mr. Browne's statement was given, after which the defendant stated that he had found the goat and had advertised that he had feund one. Be did not assault the complainant. He stated that the goat would be given up to Mr. Pennington if it Was sent for in a proper manner, and the cost of its maintenance while it had been in his possession refunded to him.—The Bench ordered the defendant to return the goat, and ordered him to pay the costs of the case. A MISSING WATCH: SINGULAR CASE OF THREATEN. iNG LANOIIAGE.—Before Messrs. George McGorcpodale, T. J. Gillespie, C. Pilkington. A. C. McColuodale, and W. F. Gooch, at the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, George Rat- cliffe, an independent gentleman residing at Earlestown, and the successful candidate in the recent election of.a Guardian for the Newton township, was summonedfor wing threatening language to William Hemmings at Earlestcrwn, on the Oth ult.—The defendant pleaded not guilty.—The complainant stated that on the date named the defendant tame to his house and wished to see him. He was in bed at the time, but his wife called him and he came downstairs. Im- mediately the defendant saw him the defendant accused bins of havlag stolen his watch, but he (complainant) at once told him that he knew nothing at all about it. The defen- dant then began to swear at him, and added that if he did not return the watch he" would knock it out of him if

.it cost a hundred pounds." lie (comP.l;,lrian-t.)-W;si-clOf the defendant doing him some harm.—ln reply to the defen- dant, complainant said he did not go to the defendant's house on the morning after the watch was missed and eay that it should be returned.—Mrs.. Remmi ngs corroborated her hus- band's evidence.—On the defendant being asked if he had anything to say, he produced a handbill announcing that a watch bad been lost on "February 23rd."—The Clerk re. marked that the paper must have been printed nearly twelve months ago.—The defendant It was six years ago.—ln. spector Comrnins : It was in 1819, your worships.—The defendant stated that after he had lost his watch and chain in 1879 he beard that it was in the complainant's possession, and on the occasion alluded to he only went to ask him if he knew anything about it. The complainant acted more like a madman than a sane man, and be (defeldant) did net threaten him Is any shape or form.—The Chairman (Colonel McCeiquodale) ultimately said: The Bench have given oareful attention to thie case and have it in evidence on oath that this man whose house you entered is in fear of you doing him bodily harm. You threatened him in the house, asked him to go out and you wauld do violence to him, and the decision is that you must be bound over in the

earn of .210 to keep the peace towards this man and all Her Majesty's subjects for the space of sta calendar months. PRaturvz METHODET Ho= Missroxs: SEustOsre AND MEETING AT EARLESTOWN.—The annual sermons on behalf of the Primitive Methodist Home Mi9BIOAS were

preached in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Legh-street, Barlestown, on Sunday morning and evening by the Rev. F. N. Shimmin, resident minister. There were fairly good congregations. In the afternoon an interesting service of song entitled "Lost Gip," was given in the school-room by the Choir of the chapel, under the leadership cf Mr. William Banton, accompanied on the harmonium by Mr. William Austin. The connective readings were given by Mr. Jame& Woods, superintendent. The service was of a very interest- ing character, and the solo parts by Miss Susan Thompson and Master F. Dickens were nicely rendered. The annual public meeting was held in the chapel on Monday evening, when there WAS a moderate attendance. The chair was oc- cupied by Mr. J. Slater, the new Town's Missionary, and he was supported by the Rev. F. N. Shimmin (resident minis- ter) and Rey. G. Morris (St. Helens). The Chairman, in opening the meeting, alluded to his experience in home mis- sion work at Salford, Manche:ter, where he had reaidod fr some time prior to coming to Earlestown. He said that the best means of reaching theimleses was by personal =Canton the part of every member belonging to the various churches. —Ha was followed by the Rev. F. N Shimmin, whn gave a statement as to the funds. He regretted that the amounts were not equal to last year, but many causes acco'arated for the deficiency, including erection of new schools during the last six months, and the fiat that the entire available force of the church bad been called into exercise to meet the requirements of the new building fund. They could not feel surprised that the amounts were 14es, seeing that during the period he bad named they ha l raif:ed over £4OO for that object, and they might fairly hope that with a little attention next year they would make their anniver- sary a greater success. The following names of the col- lectors during the past year were anncunce3 :—Miss Ada Morris, Miss Rhoda Massey, Miss Lucy Pendrey, Miss Dora Dickens, Mrs Sproston, and Mr Peter Thompson. The Rey G Morris-(St Helens), gave an excellent address on the principles and aims of Christianity. On the motion of Mr Dagnall., seconded by Mr Dobson, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the collectors for their services during the past year, and a similar compliment was paid to the chair- man on the mo1.;-n uf Mr W Idolyooke, seconded by Mr Peter ThOrnpson.

BRUNSWICK 7.r2sr.vvesr Surrnev Szsoau—On Thursday evening, a meeting of the teachers and, officers was held to consider the present state of Sunday School work, and what could be done to make it more successful. After the meet- ing, an enjoyable supper was partaken of.

THE GUARDIAN Euscrrors. BESULT OF THE POLLING. In some circles the result of the election of a member of the Board of Cvardians to fill the vacancy in the representa- tion of the Newton township has created considerable sur- prise. Recent proceedings of the Board of Guaedians in re- lation to the Newton township, particularly in reference to the prosecutions under the Vaccination Acts, gave rise to SOITIS3 bitter feeling among a portion of the inhabitants, and the local branch of the Anti-Commlsory Vaccination So- ciety actively bestirred themselves in the election proceed- ings, and nomanated a " champion " in the person of Mr. John Clarke, irontnonger, Bridge-street, Earlestown. Other four candidates were also proposedi namely, Mr. Thomas Kilehaw, Creae-lane, gentleman.; Mr. Joseph Pennington, farmer and Sniffier, Winwick Mr. George Ratcliffe, 75, Sankey-street, Earlestown, gentleman' and Mr. James Sankey, wheelwright, High-street, Newton. Shortly after the annonncement that. five candidates were in the feld, seeking the suffrages of the rate- payers, handbills were issued stating tSat "The Ex- ecutive of the Anti-Vaccination Society, being de- termined that the odium of having caused a competition for the office-of Guardian shall not be laid to their charge, have withdrawn their nominee, Mr. John Clarke, and have de- cided to vote unanimously for- Mr. George Ratcliffe, a gen- tleman who is largely interested in the rates and who is opposer:lto prosecutions for non-vaccination, and also en- tirely in faVour of medical freedom. They would therefore advise all members and friends of the Anti-Vaccination Society to vote for the candidate named above." This action on the part of the anti-vaccinationists united their forces, and as one man they appeared to 'plump " for Mr. Ratcliffe, who secured election by an overwhelming majority. The voting papers (1,997 in number) were de- livered on Thursday vmek, collected on the Friday, and. on Saturday last, they were examined and counted at the Ww- rington Workhouse by Mr. J. C. Sutton, clerk to the Guar- dians, who officiated as the returning officer for the election. The candidates and a. few of their friends and supporters were present. The result of the polling was ultimately declared as follow : Ratcliffe 521 Sankey Pennington Kilsbaw _
The success of Mr. Ratcliffe has occtsio-n-e-d the greatest satisfaction amongst his supporters, and the anti-vaccina- tionists take it as an evidence of the strong hold they have upon the community.

NEWTON COMMISSIONERS. ANOTHER FRUITLESS MEETING. The monthly meeting of the Newton Improvement Com- missioners was to have been held at the Town Hall, New- ton, on Monday afternoon, but no business could be tran- sacted, on hi to the absence of a quoram. There were pre- sent Mes.srs W F Gooch (chairman), T J Gillespie,•l3 B Glover, and r Stone, and Messrs J E Woreley (law clerk), R Brierley (surveyor), and Dr Watkins (medical officer of health). In the course of a desultory conversation which took place-among the gentlemen present, it was stated that Mr Hunt was il, Mr McCorquodale was away, and Mr Par- dey had left the town that morning.--TlMrWorsley said there was not very much business to transact as far as he was aware.—The Chairman : It is a pity another mem- ber is not tiresent.—Mr Gillespie thought it was quite time something should be done. They ought not to be called up time after time and then no quorum attend.—Mr Stone thought it would be a good plan if on the notice ' ptper for future meetings was an intimation that if any member could not attend it was advisable to acquaint the surveyor with the fact.—The Chairman thought if the matter was mentioned at the next meeting something might be done.—lt wan understood that the monthly meeting of the Board should bs held on Monday next. WATER AND GAS Irnis.--The Gas and Water Commit, tee held a meeting on the 19th ult. at which, on the report of the Surveyor, it was ordered that the water main from Upper Earle-street be extended along Wharf-road to the Ship Inn, Ne*ton Common. It was resolved that that part- of Park Side lying south of the Manchester and Liverpool railway, Newton township botmlary on the east, and Win- wick branch railway on the north-west, be a separate dis- trict for water supply purposes under section 211, sub-section 4, Public Health Act, 1875. HIGHWAY AND SANITARY CommirrEn.—At a meeting of the Highways, Public Works, and Sanitary Committee on the 19th ult., the special committed reported their inspae- tion of the disinfecting apparatus in connection with the Health Department of the Manchester Corporation, and at the Monson Infectious Hospital, and recommended that the system in use by the Manchester Health Department be adopted by the Commissioners. It was ordered that the Surveyor be instructed to prepare a plan and estimate for a disinfecting stove to be erected at the gas works on the hot air system, in use by the Corporation of Manchester. The Surveyor reported that be had arranged with the nightsoil contractor (Mr. William Ellam) to remove the contents of all privies and pails during the night for the remaining term of his contract, and that he be allowed an additional £5, per year on the same being done to the satisfaction. of the Commissioners. TELE ATTEMPTED !AMMAR OP Two CHILDREN.—At the Central Criminal Court, London, on. Wednesday, Emily Redstone, servant, was charged with attempting to drown Amy and Maud Weir, in the Thames, at Chiswick, on De- cember 31. The two children gave evidence, stating that while they were out walking the prisoner pushed them into the water. The prisoner was found. guilty, Lut the jury re- commended her to mercy. Sentence was deferred.

MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. A special meeting of this Council was held on Tuesday evening "to confirm the propriety of the promotion by the Mayer, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the borough of War- rington. in conjunction with othe-s, of a local and personal Bill in Parliament for the purpose of incorporating a com- pany and empowering such conpany to construct a canal Irom the river Mersey to the city of Manchester. navigable for °cam steamers and ships of large burthen, and the con- tribution out of the ba.oush rate to the cost of such promo- tion of a sum not excerling twopence in the pound upon the annual rateable value of the borough for one year.' Amougst the Mayor's communications was a letter from the Home Secretary, having reference to the proposed 23 rate. The letter, after setting forth the objects of the rate, dc., concluded as follows:—"!, the Right Honourible Sir William Vernon Harcourt, by virtue of the power entrusted to me by the statue aforesaid, do hereby signify my appro- val of the said resolution of the Town Council of the borough of Warrington, so far as it relates to matters with- in the jurisdiction of the Secretary of State. In witness whereof I have hereunto set my hand at Whitehall, this seventeenth day of January, eighteen hundrea anceseighty- -flve.—W. V. HARCO'URT." A motion, to the above effect was made by the MAYOR, who said that the subject had been so thoroughly thrashed out that it would be a waste of time to go into further par- ticulars. He might say, however, that flooding would be entirely obviated, se scientific men told them' if the canal were made. If it was for no other reason than that, the contribution of £4003 would be money well spent if they could prevent the unfortunate recurrence of floods on land in this neighbourhood. (Hear, hear.) Alderman CHANDLEY seconded the motion, which on being put was voted for by Aldermen Pickmere and Chan& ley, Councillors Barker, Brown, Wright, Bolton, Ashton, Francomb, Hutchinson, Tinsley, J. Pierpoint, Whittle, Fleming, Dixon, and Roberts. The only member who stood up in opposition was Coun- cillor Milner, but it was noticed that Alderman Holmes, Aldei man Webster, and Councillor Eroadbent did not vote for the motion. The MAYOR declared the molan to be cerried by a large majority. RUNCORN AND THE SHIP CANAL. A POLL DEMANDED. A special meeting of the Runcorn Board of Commission- ers was held at the Town Hall on Thursday morning, Mr. B Shaw presiding, for the purpose of considering the Man- chester Ship Canal Bill.—Mr. Pritchard said the object of the opposition was simply to secure causes to pretect the interests of the port, and he moved a resolution authorising tee Board to oppose the Bill.—Mr. P. Speakman seconded the resolution, and it was carried unanimously. On Thursday evening a ratepayer's meeting was held in Bethesda Scbool-room. The room was well filled. Mr. It. Shaw presided, and amongst these present were Dr. Mc- Doegall, Messrs. James Handley, JP., F. Bigbv, J.P., S. Taylor, W. Hayes, T. Handley, R. Davies (solicitor. War- rington). E. A. Chorlton, W. Whittaker, F. Briscoe. J. Meedowcroft, J. R. Frith, W. Dobson, P. Speakman. W. Handley, S. C. Beckett, J. Bridgewater, W. Fisher, J. W. Lightbern, J. Pritchard, J. F. Adams, H. Coleburn, J. K. Digges, J. N. Lello, Jordan, W. Sutton, W. Farrell, M. Barker, W. Brookes (secretary to the Commissioners), dm. Dr. McDorneeee inquired whether all the legal formalities had been complied with, and whether the notice convening the meeting was posted upon the Parish Church door on the previous Sunday. The Climaxes said if the Commissioners had not issued the notices properly they would be responsible, and it was not a question he should allow them to discuss there. Dr McDounkee said the chairman was in the hands of the meeting and it was not for him to say what should be discussed. If he did not submit to the meeting be should propose a formal resolution upon the matter. (Applause.) If he was not prepared to submit to the ruling of the meeting then they would have to take more stringent measures. The CHAIRMAN called upon Mr Pritchard to move a resolution, hut Dr McDougall continued speaking, and said the Commissioners must comply with the Act of Parlia- ment. As a ratepayer be declined to be bound by the re- sponsibility ot the Commissioners—they had had enough of that laeely. (Applause). The CHAIRMAN said the Act of Parliament had been complied with. Dr MeDonoAte then re-iterated hie question whether the notices had been posted apcn the Parish Church door. Mr W HANDLEY said there was no notice referring to the meeting upon the Parish ehurch door on Sunday last. The CHAIRMAN: It might have been taken off. The notices had been posted upon all the churches and chapels in the town. Dr MeDoroAet said he should divide the meeting upon the question whether the notices had been posted properly. (Applause). The Crummier remarked that they must clearly -under- stand that it did not matter to the Cernmissiners whether they passed the resolutions or not. All they would get then Would be a wall round the docks of Runcorn. Dr. MeDonoArm: You are going outside the question altogether. (Loud cries of " Chair.") The CHAIRMAN (continuing) stated that if the Board had not complied with the requirements of the Act of Parlia- ment, they would be personally responsible for any money they had spent. After that statement they could prevent the meeting if they liked, but they would only deprive the Commissioners of assistance in obtaining proper facilities for the town. It did not matter to him in the least it the docks were closed up next dl7, because his interests were On the other side of the river. Dr. MCDOUGALL here interrupted amid loud cries of chair, and moved that the chairmin 63 not allowed to pro- deed until the question was answered. Mr Lreorriemees said this was really a side issue. If they I rejected the resolutions on their merits there was an end of the matter. Mr W Scram (parish clerk), said the notice of the me* I ing was posted upon the Parish Church door on Sunday ' the 250, but last Sunday the notice bad disappeared. The CHAIRMAN still contended that this was not a ques- tion for that meeting, it was a mere quibble to divert at- tention from Le proper subject. Mr PRITCHARD, amid some confusion, said it was time they got to the business which they were met to consider. He thought it was a pity to lose so much time. (Cries of "Question," aid cheers.) The matter was in their own hands, and if they did not want to give the powers asked for. and if they did not want to protect their own interests, they need not vote for the resolution he was about to move. As a body of Commissioners, they had nothing personally t 3 gain. They bad no personal or selfish ends to tank. They were there in the interests of the ratepayers, and they had been studying and working hard for six weeks or two months to safeguard the interests of the retepayers of Runcorn. It was intended that the Manchester Ship Canal should ap- proach Runcorn along the present bed of the Mersey and Irwell Canal, aryl the Old Quey Canal would be made of the required width and depth. As soon as it approached the estuary at the Old Quay it was proposed to construct an embankment or stone wall from that point to the ter- minus of the canal at Foghorn. This embankment would be made around Runeern shore so as to admit of the canal being about 200 feet wide. It was intended to pass under the bridge about the middle of the first span, and the total length of the canal and the embankment from the Old Quay to Eastham would be 14 miles, or from the Duke's Dock to Eestham would be a little short of 12 miles. It was intended to construct this embankment to a height of six feet above the spring tides, and it was proposed to pl lee in the ernbankments numerous weirs,. each about 100 font long, to the height of an ordinary neap tide—thatie a 13 feet tide at Liverpool—so that they should, at all states of the tide, have about 9 feet of water at their deck gates and along their river walls. The object of these weirs was to admit the rising tides to flow into the canal and to flow back out of the canal until it reached the level of the weirs. He should have said that the canal was to be 26 feet deep below the tops of the weirs. They would now wish to know bow the craft tradirg in and out of Runcorn was to have access to and from the river. It was proposed to construct locks—or lock-ways, as termed in the Bill— one on this side of the railway bridge opposite the Parish Church, and another one opposite the entrance to the Duke's Docks. Now it would be evident to everyone that with this embareiment wall and a lock-way here and there that they would not have the same facility for their traffic from the river to the docks nor from the docks to the river which they had at present. It was with the greatest diffi- MIRY that inward-heund vessels were now docked and ontwartheound vessels were got away during the limited time the tide would allow. If they took into con- sideration the delay in crossing the Ship Canal and the im- pediment of a leck-way, then be said without fear of con- tradiction that it would be iclpossible to conduct the traffic of their docks. They might say, "We have the alternative of pine and coming along the new Ship Canal." Yes, but on what condition? Take the case of china clays and stone, which constituted their principal import. The charges per ton were to be : canal toll Is 61, ship dues el, wharfage 51, and a charge for towage on the canal would probably be made. The proposed works would seri- ously affect the trade of the port, and there were no clauses in the Bill at all adapted to sufficier tly protect the interests of Runcorn, and they could not sit quietly down and allow a company formed avowedly for the purpose of benefiting Warrington, Manchester, and other towns, to saddle Run- corn with heavy charges which would ruin their trade. They had the freedom of the Mersey at present to sail from their decks and Piers without toll or charges. Runcorn was already in posseseion of considerable advantages, and he did not think the ratepayers were prepared to give them Ine or allow them to be taken away for the benefit of other places. (Cbstra.) He referred to the importance of the town's sewerage works being properly protected, and said the committee appointed by the Commissioners had drafted clauses, which they deemed necessaty to protect the present and hours trade of the port, and these clauses would be submitted to the promoters, if the meeting passed the reso- lution before them. He therefore moved 'That the consent of the owners and ratepayers of the Improvement Act die. trict of Runcorn be, and the same is hereby given to the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners to oppose in Parlia- ment -.private Bill now before Parliament intituled a Bill to authorise the construction of a Ship Canal to Manches- ter and for other purposes, and this meeting approves and sanctions the applying the general district rate or other the public funds or rates uneer the control of the said Improve- Meld Commissioners to the payment of costs and expenses attendirg erteh opposition." Mr. F. RIGBY seconded the resolution. If they did net
