- expect from the promoters of the Manchester Ship Canal

(Cheers.) Mr. JAMES DOBSON supported the resolution. The Com- missioners were large ratepayers' and their interests were identical with those of the rest of the ratepayers. (Hear, hear.) The CHAIRMAN said he would mention briefly what were the clauses they proposed to introduCe into the Bill if that meeting gave them the requisite authority. In the first place, they sought to prevent any higher charges being levied than were paid already if the Ship Canal Com- pany bought the property of the Bridgewater Navigation Company. In the second place, if the Ship Canal Company built a wall as intended, the captain of any vtesel should elect whether he should go into the river at docks through the channel or not; and if he found any difficulty in going into the river he should go through the Company's channel free of any charge whatever. (Cheers.) In the next place, the company should find any motive power necessary for taking craft across to the river from the docks, if cattail:as of vessels sought to go. They also sought to get clauses with respect to sewage. The Chairman then put the resolution, but there were loud cries from the body of the room in favour of Dr. McDomeeme addressing the meeting. He said he was sorry he could not sympathise with the observations just made in respect to the Ship Canal. About three or four years ago they had a meeting in support of this very scheme in that room, and subsequently representatives of the Commissioners were sent to London to watch over the retepayere interests, and they came back and presented a modest little bill for payment of expenses. (Laughter.) A little while after that there was a sort of flourish of trum- pets, in the shape of pamphlets issued to householders, and a meeting was held at. Waterloo House. A procession was there formed, which reminded one of the pied piper. They would remember there was a strong feeling about the second deputation going to Loterlon. However, they did go, and whether they submitted their resolution or not they had £B2 to pay out of the rates for three individuals in London. They received £l2 as a bonus upon the la, clerk's charges, which they admitted. The CHAIRMAN: There is not a bit of truth in it. After a little altercation Dr McDouteeee resumed his address, and severely criticised the Commissioners upon their delay in the matter. He read a clause of the Bill with respect to the protection of vessels. Supposing the promo- ters were going to construct a canal which would bring Into Runcorn vessels of 1,500 to 2 000 tons, would it be reasonable to expect these to come in without paying the balance upon vessels of 500 tons, which were the largest that could now enter the port? The fact was the Ship Canal would do away with monopoly. The Bridgwater Navigation Company were monopolists. They could not, get a ton of goods into Runcorn by the Bridgewater Canal or by railway under 2e 6,1; and anything they could do to cheapen the rates would be a geed thing. He was quite , sure the promoters would not do anything to injure the trade of Runcorn, and the ratepeyers were not prepared in the present state of trade to spend £3OO in expenses. Mr LELLO said they were summoned theta to speak on a I matter of great moment, but the Chairman had tried to gag the months of the ratepayers. (Hear, heir.) I Mr ROBERTS :We won't let the minority rule the majn, ity this time. (Cheers). Mr. LELLO said Runcorn was burdened sufficiently with rates, and he was pleased to think that meeting would say they would nut allow things to go on in the future as they had in the pest. He could not trust the Commissioners so much as they seemed to trust themselves. Loud laughter and cheers.) The CHAIRMAN: I must ask you, gentlemen, whether the conduct of the Commissioners is to he discussed in this way? After some further discussion and confusion, Mr. ROBERTS said he would propese, as an amendment, that if the Commissioners go to London they pay their own expenses. (Laughter.) He added that the Commissioners would only contradict each other as they did at Chester. (Laughter.) Mr. J. W. LIGHTBURN defended the action of the Com- missioners. He thought it was too bad after they had spent their time and money, and worked hard, to be treated as they had. The Commissioners had nothing but the interest of the ratepayers at heart. The CHAIRMAN explained that the words of himself and Mr. Pritchard had been misconstrued when they spoke of not caring. They plainly said that they, personally, did not care ; that it was no interest to them personally. He did not believe there was any pri- vate house in Runcorn assessed so high as his own, 80 that for every shilling that was spent he would be the largest contributor. The motion was then put to the meeting. Only 27 persons voted in favour, there being a large ma- jority against the resolution. The Cnernerex declared that the resolution was not carried. Mr. W. Powreeee, SM., said the ratepayers were not re- presented that evening, and he begged to propose that a poll be taken. He could see the bread and cheese of the working-men sailing past Runcorn if the Ship Canal became law, and he demanded a poll. (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN: I !hall make arrangements for taking a poll on tees question. (Applause) The meeting then commenced the consideration of the Gas Bill

MEETING OF THE PROVISIONAL COSIMITTEE.—The weekly meeting of the Provisional Committee was held in the Boardroom. 70i, Market street, Manchester, yesterday afternoon. Mr. Henry Boddington, jun. presided. A communication was submitted from a firm Of shipowners in Liverpool affording substantial support to the scheme, as also from other sources. The proceedings of the Parlia- mentary Sub-committee were r;ported, from which it appeared that every preparation is being made far the forthcoming inquiry. The nature of the evi- dence to be laid before Parliament, and the selection of witnesses to be called on behalf of the scheme, has occupied their attention, and all necessary steps are being vigorously pushed forward to present a strong case. The decision of the Mersey Dock and Harbour Board to op- pose the Bill in the face of the pledges given in Parliament last session not to oppose a Bill next session if the canal were carried along the Cheshire side (as proposed in this year's plans) instead of down the centre of the estuiry as previously proposed, was referred to. On the part of the public this decision appears to have been received with con- siderable dissatisfaction and indignation. Resolutions passed by the Corporations of Heywood, Bury, and Macclesfield were submitted in support of the scheme appointing the Mayors of these towns to give evidence en behalf of their Corporations. Sr. HELENS AND THE SHIP CANAL.—OH Wednesday a special meeting of the St. Helens Town Councilt was held, at which a resolution was prooosedauthorising thetown clerk to oppose the Ship Canal in -Parliament in order to protect ' the interests of St. He'ens. The motion was, however, not sapported by a sufficient majority, and the meeting conse- quently proved abortive.
Thr Birkenhead Town Council resolved on Wednesday, by 38 votes to three, to oppose the Manchester Ship Canal Bill.

At a meeting of the Salford Town Council, on Wednes- day, it was resolved that the Mayor (Alderman R. Makin. son), the Es-Mayor (Alderman Husband), Alderman Wa'matey, and the borough engineer give evidence in the coming session of Parliament in favour of the Ship Canal Bill.

div.head: TRADE DEPRESSION: A FEW REMEDIES. BY IL WHITMAN'.
div.p: TRADE DEPRESSION: A FEW REMEDIES. BY IL WHITMAN'.

Your columns, alike with those of your contemporaries, have been recently teeming with letters and articles on Trade depression. Various reasons are given for tke pre- sent depressed state of things, and various are the remedies suggested. One, and that the least feasible, Fair Trade, his been thrashed pretty near thread-bare. Its exponents, after stating that they wish for Free Trade as keenly as any- one, go on differing very much as to what they mean by Fair Trade, one writer, a Mr. Turner, stating that he'will never rest until we have Protection all round. Mr. Jas. Lowther, speaking at Darlington, said :—" 1 foresaw the time when a 5s duty would be useless, when the sliding scale would have to go, as it would this year had one existed, up to lOs per quarter:, to be of any advantage." The Rt. hon. gentle- man, like most Fair Traders, is very hazy, and falls to convey his real meaning as to what portion of the commu- nity is likely to receive the " advantage," when it would be impossible to buy wheat at lees than 45s per quarter. These remedies prove to a certainty how these Fair traders are living " up in a balloon." It is one thing to try to introduce Protection ; it is a far more serious thing to ignore the many and the obvious reasons why we are having such long seasons of depression, followed by short seasons of briskness. Very few writers could sit down, and state off-hand, all the reasons why we have bad trade ; nor could any man give satisfaction after so stating his reasons. To the teetotaller it is sufficient to advise the taking of the pledge, and it must be granted, that, were the money that is spent in bear spent in clothing, the Lancashire and Yorkshire mills would be having rare times of it. The land reformers say—mend your land laws, and then, instead of England's peasantry flocking into the towns, they would have better and healthier work in the country. This also is true, for is it not a fact that all the mill gates throughout Lancashire are besieged by hungry mcii anxious to earn an honest livelibood? These and several other remedies are needed, and it is very desirable public attention should be directed towards them.

~....-...- —......._ ......... Yet there are other, and not less distinctive, features connected with trade that it seems to me equally necessary to attend to. The question of railway traffic rates is one that calls for, and urgently demands immediate attention. Mr. Adamson, of ship canal fame, recently stated that the rates were becoming so excessive that unless something was done cipitalists would be driven out of the country. In 1872, Sir W. Watkin promised the Manchester Chamber of Commerce that dividends should be limited to five percent; yet eight and nine per cent have been paid. Sc. per ton is paid for cotton on the Bridgewater Canal, yet the old Bridgewater Act only authorises Os per ton. By a fiction of law, railways and canals are prohibited from being managed and controlled by the same companies, and yet it is well known the same gentlemen sit on the boards of management controlling railways and canals. The railway companies are at the present time, by a number of bills, seeking to increase their already over-grown powers.

As an example of bow the people suffer by exorbitant rail way rates, I may mention that twenty•nine boat loads of sprats were wasted at Inverness the other day because the cost of transport to London was so great as to be prohibi- tive. It costs 12s. to send a barrel of herrings from the

north of Scotland to London, while the freLy;ht -from Scot- land to Russian ccmes to no more than 2. Clearly the railway question is one for & People's Parliament to deal with. I see it stated that the "paid-up capital of:our rail- ways to the end of 18E6 was £784,000,000, of _ which
£196,000.000 consisted of debentures,. stOcks;_and.loans,

£93,000,000. of ordinary stock, and the rest of preference - and guarantieed. stocks." An increase therefore of one per cent divided on the ordinary stocks of the railways mean - an additional impost on the traders of the kingdom of nearly. three millions sterling per annum, and yet a Burnley mill man iger advises a twenty per cent reduction in cotton opera.. tives wages r And new to turn to another feature that may possibly have more to do with our bad times than we -think of. I refer to commercial morality. For years past it has been the habit of writers, on working-men's questions, to roundly I charge them with "scarnping " their work. In the build- ing trade words sufficiently strong could scarcely be fount to hurl at the poor plumbers and joiners. Whenever anything went wrong with either drain pipes or gas pipes the work- mate was in fault. It could never be acknowledged that possibly a too low tender had something to do with it, and that this would account for the hurry-scurry and " ecamping "of the work. Witness our new workhouse schools ; had this job been kept in the town ratepayers would have been some hundreds of pounds in pocket. John Bright writes :--" Our morality is not by any means what I would like to see it." Mr. Thomas Hughes, QC., speak- ing at Manchester, says :—" The keenest an least scrupu- lous, instead of the wisest and most upright of men, had come to the front, and got to the front of almost every branch of industry and trade. He did not say that the time had actually come when an honest and scrupulone man could not live by trade, Istit it was not far off." These are hard words, but there is quite sufficient in the history of the cofton trade to justify them ; I may also include the wool- len trade. ,A writer states that the adulteration of cotton goods is of a " character to seriously affect the health, not of the half-castes of India, poor Chieeso, or the African negro, but of the working-men of this cauntry, and their families. Some manufacturers, for no earthly reason but to reduce the price of the cloth by /I or p per lb., and thus enable them to undersell toe honest manufacturer, take the piece of waste twill sheeting, put it through a process by which a revolving brush sends over every part of the material a spray of antiseptic liquid or other chemical which will neither mildew nor dry, and which answers their purpose by adding from 5 to la per cent of weight to the piece which they sell by the pound. The saving in a pair of sheets is from ld to 3,1, and in the lining of a pair of trousers Id to Id." So we' see our manufacturers turn out goods which uted as lining for trousers never dry, and if put on the bed unwashed, as sheets " absorb moisture in the day and give it off to the tired limbs of the worker at night." Twills also are made firm, thick, and heavy, with China clay. It seems to me the remedy is in our own hands. Manufacturers are in too big a hurry to get rich. There are yet other causes at work that account in a measure for our depression. Allow me now to qlote from an article by Colonel Philips, Commissioner-General of the Bombay Army. Writing under the heading " What ails Trade;' and speaking from a large Indian experienc>, he says it is not over-production, but because we will not take whet money the Indian has in his pocket, but compel him to change it for gold, with this result i "Our customers in silver-esing countries will no longer buy from us what they can either make themselves, or buy from more accommo- dating people." In Bombiy scores of mills have been built for making cotton cloth, and the present rate of exchange is stimulating this industry. Five large mills are at present going up, and practically all yarns under 303 are made in India for the Indian market, and compete with Manchester yarns and cloths in China, on the East coast of Africa, and in Aeletic countries generally. Thus we see it is no ques- tion of Fair Trade, but one of simple business. Skilled su- pervisien, machinery, and coal have to be imported from England, and naturally Lancashire trade goes with them, because " Eegland refuses to take rupees in payment for cotton manufactures." The same writer says be entered iato contracts for blankets in 1883, which were to b 3 made in India, and for the Indian troops, and that shortly the weaaing of broad cloth will hastened, and all this in order that peOple with fixed incomes may enjoy the benefits of dear gold at home. Iron and steel are next on the list. "If the iron-masters of England are debOrred much longer from taking Indian rupees for their iron and steel such a premium will be put on the manufacture in leedia as must sooner or later foster Indian Competition: Now see what this Indian Colonel says in conclusion :—" I hope that my ad- vice will not be taken, and that England will continue to refuse her customers money, if it be silver, for my stipend is paid in gold, and I like to get twenty-two or twenty-three shillings' worth for my sovereign at your expense." Will the warning be taken?

The assertion, though it may be from a teetotaller, is plausible, but certainly incorrect ; when the wine at the last supper is referred top this point 'shall not bo-lost stbt of.

In conolusion,li wish to point out to " Moderator " that whether he fails in proving his positipn or not, it will nct affect mine; P shalt still be secure. For the third time I venture to assert that even if there were nothing we might learn on this question from the bible, and even if it can be proved that Christ was not an abstaiiar, our position is vin- dicated by facts of science and personal experie.m.* too plait to be misunderstood. These being opposed to the theories of " Moderaterli."party, they are obliged as,a last resort to fly to the bible, where they try to hide themselves behind the assertion that it is an " historical fact " that Christ was not a teetotiller,thereby attempting to justify themselves in habitually drinking the two or three hundred varieties of so-called wine—from the mildest claret to the highly forti- fied ports and sherries; a vast proportion of which has never been associated with the juice of the grape even to the smallest degree. , • As "Moderator has undertaken to prove that Christ was not a teetotaller, I am content for the prefent, at joist, to allow him to try to do so. I may endeavour to give hull some grounds. for my belief in a while.—Yaores respect- fully, TEE TEE. Aerlestovmq.2nd Feb4lBBs. .

div.head: Xetten to the Odttor-.-
div.p: Xetten to the Odttor-.-
MORE SCANDAL AT THE PARISH CHURCH.

Sir,—Yes; more scandal ; and when shall an end be put to this state of things? Is it not high time? Scarcely a month or even a week passes without some discreditable proceeding being brought to light. What does it all mein? Have all the parishioners of the Warrington Parish Church lost their heads? It wauld appear so, inasmuch as there is none," no not one," who has the moral courage to protest or raise a voice against a stite of things that has long ago bicome intolerable ; and yet those two worthies, "the war- dens," wink at this sort of thing. Where are all the "shining lights "—I mean the " upper crust "? Do they know the Parish Church too well ? But stay, Mr. Editor, I grievously err. I forgot for the moment that we have no " shining lights "—no " upper crust who attend the Sabbath services there. Time was when carriage after carriage drove up to the gates of this ancient house of prayer, and Church-street on a Sabbath mom pre- sented a somewhat different spectacle to what it does at the present time. Why is it not so now ? For years a system of persecution has been carried on with impunity by those who ought to know better; and it is a well-known fact that these scandal-mongers dwell not a hundred miles from the church's very doors. No doubt, sir, you will before long have occasion to place before your readers some start- ling particulars respecting the "mysterious inner circle " who manage affairs at the Parish Church. Until thea I will be silent, and will content myself by saying that for a long time past things have been in anything but a satis- factory condition—in fact they have been all "hustle and cenfusion."—Yours, ALPHA. Warrington, 4th February, 1885.

div.head: TEETOTALISM AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: TEETOTALISM AT EARLESTOWN.

Sir,—l should like to say at the outset that I rather regret the limitations to which the discussion under the above heading has been drawn ; it seems to have lost much of its interest, but I suppose the style the discussion was drifting into has made this inevitable. Let me say here I have no desire whatever to pose as the champion of the teetotal cause In Eariestown. I have no doubt there are others who are better qualified to defend the cause than such a humble in- dividual as myself, but again, I suppose we must accept the inevitable, and having gone so far, I mnst try in my own feeble way to defend my principles and the position I take on this question, and when lam defeated, or annihilated, retire quietly into obscurity again. And now to the question at issue, for [ beg to inform " Moderator "that I mean " serious business," though I certainly did think he had Wen serious from the first, for I can assure him I have been. His last letter is far from be- ing a reply to mine of the 24th. He is evading altogether the pertinent points and questions I proposed to him, and I ask him to compare the two letters a little. "Moderator," in rather domineering style, refers again to his authorities on the social habits of the Jews, &c. Now, as I am not a bookseller, or librarian, or quite so well off as our friend " Moderator," I do not possess the works mentioned, nor do I believe one in a hundred of your readers do either—but, even if they could be borrowed, I consider it most unreason- able for "Moderator "to expect that lOr anyone else can wade through the works mentioned from one end to the other in order to find out what is said on this question, quote the words, and then reply to them afterwards. Citing the works instead of the words of his authorities is what I referred to when I stated I received a stone in answer to my request for bread ; this is now confirmed. It is quite fair and honourable for me to say that if " Moderator " will kindly give us Dr. Geikie's facts, Dean Stanley's arguments and Dr. Blackie's reasons, providing they have some bearing on the question at issue, viz—that Christ was not a teetotaller—l promise, as far as my humble abilities will allow me, 0 reply to them, or say that I can- not.

With respect te his teetotal proofs, I beg to say that I am not prepared to adopt as facts, or as truth, the opinions an theories of every teetotaller, any more than these of every Christian, nor would " Moderator." If we did, we should be at sea directly. The remarks of the Rev. E. Day—now before me, are very conflicting in their charac- ter ; when all is summed up, he can only give his opinion what he thinks was probable, that the wine used at the " feasts " of public Ins and sinners was probably intoxicating in its character; and this is all that " Moderator" can do. There is literally no proof that our Saviour drank wine at all on the occasion referred to. As I stated in my last, we want facts not theories, proofs not opinions, unless we can bare same better foundation for them than that given, and I once more tender to " Moderator" the two propositions in my last letter,--first, that Christ actually partook of wine, and, secondly, that the wine so partaken was a'cobulic or intoxicating in its character ; to th.s3 I expect a reply in his next, or a confession that he cannot, for I beg to in- form him that I mean "serious business." It may be very convenient for " Moderator " to style my view of the " new wine " as very plausible and incorrect, but it still needs confuting. " Moderator " has not attempted to reply to It, and I ask him to read the paragraph referred to, and let me know where lam incorrect, and where the sophistry lies. The words of the authority he quotes (Rev. F. A. Malian!), M.A.) have no reference whatever to the "new wine in new wine bags," but to the wine in the cup at the last supper at Easter, a point not yet raised, at which I am rather sur- prised, for it is certain that our Saviour did on that Occa- sion partake of wine; but I shall try to deal with that ques- tion when it is introduced.

It seems rather conflicting for " Moderator " to say he will not now discuss the impossibility of grape juice being kept without fermenting, and then to follow with an au- thority whose point is that juice expressed in the previous autumn could not have been preserved without fermenting.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON? THURSDAY.

There certainly cannot be complaint made of. what is called the dead season. The whiter of 1.884-5 would be memoralate, if for nothing else, for the unusual liveliness of the times. We have had an autumn session, a war full of incident, a succession of dynamite explosions, and for this wer.k's sensational incident, apart from the fall of Khar- toum, we have the shooting of O'Donovan Rossa. When Rossa reads the newspapers, as he undoubtedly will, for he is a man of infinite vanity; he will doubtless be gratified to find the unanimity with which the civilised world wish that he were dead. English papers, strained to control their feel- ings, have not given expression to the common desire. But the American journals, more free spoken, have watched by the bed-side of the wounded bravo undiszniaedly wishing that his injury might prove fatal. This wish has not been gratified. The toy pistol that Mu. Dudley handled did scarc-.ly any harm except that it has lifted this skulking coward on a pinnacle of which he knows how to take the most advantage. It is admitted that Mrs. Dudley's shot is worth anything to Roma, and since it did no particular harm people are beginning to wiskit had never been fired. Affairs have taken a new turn in'the Soudan by the startling news which reaches L.ondoa this afternoon of the capture of Gordon. It seems at the end of a diflicult and desperately played game to leave the Mandi master of the situation. Whilst lamentin.e, the catastrophe, ills imp3s- sible not to admire the subtlety of the Arabs. No one can say how long they have had Khartoum in their hands. There were weeks or even months ago rumours which caused feelings of uneasiness. It was stated that Khartoum had already fallen and that Gerdon was a prisoner. It teems now as if there were too much reason to believe that these reports were true. However that be It is certain that

the fall of Khartoum was not a matter of yesterday, and all this time it has been kept a profound secret whilst the British army has been cunningly lured forward into the ambush prepared for it. From that, at least Sir C. Wilson leas escaped. But this news changes the whole aspect of aff Are and there is too much reason to fear that we are now only Ceginning a businese that seemed to have bean prac- ticaely closed. Sir Stafford Northcote has been pliantly sticking at his silf-appointed task of rousing Conservatiem in Devonshire, the campaign culminating in his pleasantly-constructed but a little obscure flower sermon. It is really very hard upon eir Stafford that he should just now have to go stumping the country. Tnis day fortnight Parliament will resume its work, and there will re-commence the long task of the treader of the Opposition in the House of Commors Sir Stifferd is not in robust health, and is specially warned against partaking in exciting scenes, an injurction certaiply carried out in respect of his many meetiege in Devonshire. But with e eiselion before him in which, though it looke quiet enough, no One can say what may happen, it would I have been wiser for, him to have taken his rest whilst it was possible. He has not even the consolation of knowing that be has done any good. As a county member, a popular English gentleman at home among his own people, Sir Stafford has been in his element. But when the House of Commons leader of a great party speaks, his words are winged for 'light far beyond the local circle in which they are spoken. Sir Stafford Northcote's speeches have not caused a ripple in the polPicel world, beyond one of mild estonishment that a capable man should speak so much mad say so little. It is very different in the case of Mr. Goechen. He has always possessed himself of that human Merest which in racing circles attaches to the dark horse. Ever since be left the Government of 1868 there has been an uncertainty, not to say a mystery, about his movements which has drawn attention upon him. When he withdraw his name from the club list of the Devonshire and the Reform m ley people were prepared to bear that he would openly hoist the Conservative colours. He stopped short of this course, and elected to come out as an Independent Liberal, which for practical purposes is not far removed from the average Conservative. His speeches have been read with great in- terest, and have been marked by all hie peculiar ability. They have, however, distinctly failed to satisfy the Liberals of Edinburgh, and if Mr. Goschen succeede in obtaining a seat in any of the divisions of the city it will be by the Conservative vote. Eventually he will drift into the Con- servative ranks, a course made much easier for him by the most recent development of Conservatism. The Coneerve- tism of the near future will be a very different thing from what it has been in the immediate past. It will, for example, be much MON Liberal than were the Liberal party in the days of Lord Palmerston. Lord Randolph Churchill, if his health permits, will be the leader of the great Conservative party. and its principles and aspirations as expounded by him will be of a character likely to make the late Lord Derby Men in his grave. With such a partv it will not be difficult for Mr. Geed:len to work, and strenuous effete will be made to enlist so useful a re- cruit. Tbe work of renovating the House of Commons after the exploits of the dynamitards is proceeding apace, and on Thursday week, when the House meets, there will reanain few traces of the outrage. Already the glass roof is re- paired, and looking upwards there is nothing to show of what has been. Very few members of the House of Come mons, and still fewer outsiders, know the mystery that lies behind this famous glass roof. Of course there are the as burners. But there is something more beyond, and that is one of the finest carved roofs in modern architecture. The glass ceiling, which serves a double purpose in lighting the House and in assisting the ventilation, was an afterthought. When the building was fi St opened for use, members looked up into its lofty heights and beheld the beautiful carving. But there was speedily discovered the correspond- ing disadvantage that little of uttered speech could be beard. The Chamber was, in respect of accoustical properties, a little worse than the House ef Lords is at the present day. All kinds of experiments were desperwely tried. One was the spreading across of a wooden ceiling somewhere abotrt the height where the glass roof is now fixed. This brought about an immediate improvement, and then came the happy thought of the glass roof, which has succeeded in making the House one of the easiest possible Chambera to speak in.

It is in fact too atttactive in this respect, and leads to occasional disturbances, people overhearing what was not intended for them. I never forget the fearful row that sud- denly burst forth one night when Nolan was on his legs. He was explainin4in his breathless excited way the reason why he bad not been in his place an hour earlier when someone he desired to hear had been speaking. " The fact is," said the gallant major confidentially; '1 have been to dinner." " He looks like it," someone murmured from the benches opposite, when instantly the whole Irish party were up in arms demanding apologies and loudly invoking the protection of the Speaker against these interruptions. Talking about the acoustical properties of the present House of Commons, I am reminded that the temporary House built after the burning of the older palace was a marvel of acoustical perfection. There still lingers a tradi- tion that Jenny Lind having heard of this characteristic, went down and put it to the test, warbling a snatch from Trovatore, to the unspeakable delight of the policemen in ckarge of the building. Jenny Lind, then in the height of her fame, declared this temporary building the best ro,-,m he had ever sang in.

Lord Sherbrooke' s second marriage has greatly tickled the fancv of his old friends who knew him as Mr Lowe. The first Mrs. Lowe was also pretty well: knOwn, though, except as an occasional diner out, in com- pany with her distinguished husband, she rarely went into society. All kiwis of stories:well invented, though doubt- less not true, were told of the state of domestic subjection in which the redoubtable Parliamentary free lance used to be kept. Mrs. Lowe certainly was a most remarkable looking person, Singularly direct in speech. She realised for me my idea of Betsy Trotwood, though not nearly so well dreesed. Failing other distinctions, Lord Sherbrooke and the late Lady Sherbrooke bore away the palm as the worst dressed couple in London. Lord Sherbrooke has within the last few years discarded his famot.s Inverness wrapper fami- liar at the epoch of the Cave of Adnllam. Oddly enough, he has done it just at the time when the Inverness is coming into fashion again, at least with evening*dresa,a very eensibie turn, as everybody will admit who has endeavoured to struggle into an ordinary overcoat with a dress coat under- neath. For th's great boon the world is indebted to the Prince of Wales, who for fully eighteen months has worn an Inverness over his evening dress when going to or frem the theatre or dinner parties.

IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE.—The fortnightly meeting of the National League was held in Dublin on Wednesday. Mr. T. P. O'Connor, M.P., said that at the general election there would be 80 or 90 Parnellite members, Etta when the time came for Mr. Parnell b make an appeal to the people for funds with which to pay the members, the result virould astonish the world. The hon. gentleman made no reference to the dynamite outrages.

div.head: L VIEST NE WS.
div.p: L VIEST NE WS.
THE FALL OF KHARTOUM. OFFICAL REPORT OF SIR CHARLES WILSON'S VISIT' TO THE CITY.

THE FATE; OF GENERAL GORDON, &c. The following is • the detailed report made by Lieutenant Stuart Wortley, who accompanied Sir Charles Wilson to Khartoum ;—We went in steamers with Sir C. Wilson to Khartoum on the 28th January, having had to run by Halfiyeh under the heavy fire of four guns and musketry. A heavy fire also opened on them from Tuti island, rind from Omdurman and Khartoum. They could not land under such opposition, so turned round and ran/down the stream. No flags were flying from the Government house in Khartoum, and the home appeared wrecked. Only one man was killed, but five were wounded in the steam- ers. On ens( 3tst January, the steamer on which were Sir C. Wilson and all his party was wrecked about four miles above the enemy's position below the bottom of the Rhabluka cataract. We reached C-übat in small boats at two p.m. the same day. The fall of Khartoum on the 26th January he reports to bo without doubt, but the fate of Gordon is uncertain, as reports are conflicting. The general opinion is-that he is killed, but there is no preponder- ance of evidence either way. Some say he is shut lupin a church in Khartoum with some Greeks. The 1 fall of Khartoum has determined the Shekrijeb 'tribes to join the Mandi, so the east bank of the Nile as well as the left bank is now hoStile to us. The fear of the English is great amongst the natives. general Earle's advance is awaited with anxiety by them. The natives say the Mandi was very hard pressed for supplies at Onadur- natl. It is said by the natives that he will have great difficulty In persuading his Emirs to attack us. A messenger from the Mandi y reached Sir Charles Wilson when on the steamer, on ; the z9th January, telling him Gordon had adapted ' the Mandi's uniform, and calling upon us to surren- der, but he would write again, and if we did not become Mahommedans he would wipe us off the LA's of the earth. It it said that Faroz Pasha treacher- ously made terms with the Mandi and opened the gata of the city to. the Mandi's troops. Lord Wolseley adds that Talbot's convoy reached Gubat safely, having left Gakdul (in the 28th Jan. The enemy at Metemmeh fired large guns on the 28th January, having evidently heard of the fall of Khartoum, but they have shown no increased ac- tivity since then. The force in Metemmeh is estima- ted between two and three thousand, of which 250 are horsemen, and from four to six hundred with rifles. The men are healthy, and the wounded doing well. At present the Kabbabish tribe have engaged to carry for us to Gakdul. He was sending mes- senger to ascertain news of Gordon. The troops at Gakdul were reported in good health, and the wounded progressing favourably DEFEAT OF THE MAHDI NEAR SENAAR

6000 ARABS KILLED. A. special correspondent of the Standard, telegraph. ing from Massowah on Tuesday, said :—The Sheik A bdel Kader, of the friendly tribe of Beniamers, has arrived here. He is the bearer of excellent news of the beleagured garrisons of the interior. His people have succeeded in carrying out the engag- ment whica they undertook, to revictual Kassala. From Ghira, on the Settit river, the news comes that the garrison hive made a successful sortie ; while in the Galliball country the Takroori tribesmen, under their Sheikh Saleb, aided by three Abyssinian Chiefs and theit followers, fought a great bat- tle with a large force of the ~Baggara rebels detached from Senaar: After a severe struggle the followers of the Mandi were utterly routed, with the loss of six thousand men, including four Emirs, one of them a nephew of the Mahal CABINET MEETING YESTERDAY. DESPATCH FROM LORD WOLSELEY._

A. --"CtTb-i-nei -CO-; di-We:ha at on Fri • day morning at the Premier's official residence in Downing-street. The Secretaries of State for War for Foreign affairs had interviews with the Premier previous to the other ministers assembling all of whom attended except Lord Spencer. The Central News is enabled to state upon undoubted authority that the ministers were called together to discuss solely the changed aspect of affairs in the Soudan consequent upon the fall of Khartoum, and to decide upon the steps now to be taken. A long telegram despatched from Lord Wolseley was submitted to the Cabinet, in which his Lordship asked for specific instructions as to the course he should pursue' Lord Wolseley laid the whole question before the Govern- ment with sufficient clearness. He peinted cud that the march upon Khartoum could still be completed, and he was perfectly ready to do that and to crash the Mabdi if the Government so ordered, but never- theless, the fall of Khartoum and the elation in the rebel ranks consequent on the victory over General Gordon and the retreat of Sir Charles Wilson, had rendered the task not only difficult but dangerous. Lord Wolseley further directed attention to the rapidly advancing season which would still fur- ther add to the hazard of the enterprise as iu a few weeks' time, the tropical heat would play havoc in the British ranks if the men were called upen for any unusual exertions. In any ease many more men would be lost from this cause than from the spears and bullets of the Arabs, and Lord Wolseley, using his utmost endeavours, could not hope to be ma plsition to make a direct assault upon Khartoum in less than five weeks when the heat would be fatal to English troops. Lord Wolesley expresses his inten- tion of drawingin his forces to some favourable posi- tion unless he is directed to continue his march against the Mahal. In pursuance of this intention General Earle has been ordered to stay any further advance and await instructions. General Buller has been similarly advised, and Lord Wolesley says he will not make any definite move until the decision of her Majesty's Government reaches him. The discussion of the situation as set forth by Lord Wolesley lasted from eleven until two o'clock, when members separated. The Central News is enabled to state that the Government decided to give Lord Wolseley carte blanche to act as he thinks best, and to adopt any measures he may think fit Lord Wols-ley will in the meantime advise the Go- vernment of the steps he proposes taking, and what be desires to be done here to assist him. NO rein- forcements will be sent unless requested by Lord Wolseley, but it is generally anticipated that a force of Indian troops will be despatched to Suakim. The Central News believes that Lord Wolseley, having a free hand allowed him, will elect for the present to concentrate his forces and make the most stringent • inquiries through native spies as to Gordon's fate before making any decided move. The.deoision of the Cabinet was immediately telegraphed to Lord Wolseley, and his Lordship was invited to telegraph his suggestions and wishes immediately. The Cabinet, on rising, decided to meet again next day, when it is expected .Lord Woleeley'S reply will have reached them, and necessary orders can then be issued according to his requirements. No arrange- , ment for the movement of troops have yet been made, I although the Transport Department have everything I in readiness to act upon the shortest notice. Lord Northbrook, Earl Granville, Earl Kimberley, I and Sir Charles Dike conferred at the Foreign Office after the Cabinet Council. The French, German, and Turkish Ambassadors had interviews with Lord Granville.. PREPARATIONS AT WOOLWICH.

Twenty. thousand boxes were yesterday called for by the Commissariat Department, and the carpenters of the Royal Laboratory were at once set to work upon them, while all that were on hand were imme- diately sent off to the provision stores in the dock- yards. Tke boxes are chiefly those used for packing meat, biscuits, tea, &c., but there are already in the reserve packed ready for issue, sufficient provisions TO fit out a new expedition of ten thousand men and keep them in rations for six weeks. It has been currently, reported to-day that a new corps d'armee of nearly that strength was to he sent out to Khar- tom by way of Abyssinia, and that a siege train manned by two or three batteries of artillery was to join part of it. The steamship Eldorado, which left the Royal Albert Docks on Friday morning, took Government stores of various kinds to Alexandra and Suez, and stopped at Gravesend -while a supply of ammunition sent from Woolwich and Purfleet were taken on board. Enquiries a*e now being made with regard to pack saddles for mules and tube wells. which lend colour to the supposition of an intended march across Abyss:nit'.

O'Donovan Rosso has been removed to a private hospital, and is doing well. John Crooks, cotton spinner, was sentenced to eight years' penal servitude at the Nottingham Assizes, for stabbing his sweetheart.
At Derby, on-Friday, the magistrates discharged the man Philip Newbold, who was charged with being concerned in • dynamite conspiracy._ _ . .

. -- - The funeral of Lord O'Hagan took place on Friday morn- ing, at the Olasnevin Cemetery, Dublin, amongst the mourners being Earl Spencer. A League meeting in IrelAnd, announced to be held on Sunday, at Idurrin Town, Wexford, bee been proclaimed by

, he Lord Lieutenant. ,te is the first meeting' m'orriaime in Wexford. At the Old Bailey, on Friday, Emily Redstone, who was I Convicted on Wednesday of attempting to drown two chit- ' dren of her mistress's at Chiswick, was sentenced to seven it years' penal servitude.

GOLBORNE.

WESLEYAN CHAPEL—On Thursday night week the Rev. J. M. Fairbourn, of Earlestown, delivered his lecture on '4 Hugh Latimer," in the above chapel, when a collection was made towards building a school and opening the chapel. Mr. Grimke presided, and there was a fair audience. The subject was ably dealt with, and as cordial vote of thanks was given to the lecturer and chairman at the close. ACCIDENT AT TILE PAPER MILL —A youth named Ent- wistle was seriously injured at the Gol borne Paper Mill on Friday morning. His shirt sleeve was caught in the machinery, and his right arm almost stripped to the bone. He was removed home, and Dr. Worsley' was speedily sum- monsed. Entwistle, who is the son of ORO of the inside managers, has met with two,previons accidents at the works, and had his collar bone broken in a football match about two years age. A REMARKABLE PRICACHEIL—A Wesleyan local preacher from St Helens, named Leach, who preached at Golborne on Sunday last, gave some interesting facts connected with his career. He said he had jest entered upon his 80th year, and for the last 50oyears he had been is constant work as a local preacher. During the first three months be preached 28 times, and travelled a distance of 250 miles. Of this journey 220 miles were made on foot. Much of his early career was spent about Runcorn and Warrington. DAMAGING A MILL.—At the Newton Petty Sessions cid Saturday before Messrs I. Jl. Gillespie, C. Pilkington, and A. C. McCorqundale, three lads named James Tittle, Augustus Allen, and Henry Hurst, were summoned for committing damage to the amount of is to timber at Gol- borne, the property of John Chadwick. Superintendent Weir explained that the case arose out of damage which had been done to an old mill in Lowton-road, Grolborne. A great deal of damage had been committed, and the agent to the property had communicated with him (Superintendent Weir) about the matter. He thereupon directed the con- stables to pay attention to it, and the result was that the boys were found damaging the timber.—The defendants were orderea to pay the danrze, and the costs. RATEPAYERS' MEETING.--Ige• New, Railway, v: An important rneetiog of ratepayers was held in Mr. Brewis' schoolroom on Wednesday evening to consider the route proposed by the promoters for the contemplated railway from St. Helens to Lowton. Mr W U Rigby presided, and there was a moderate attendance. The Chairman called upon Mr. Peter Garton to introduce the business. Mr Garton said the company in question usually called their stations central, but as regards Uolborne the proposed line would be half a mile from the centre of the township. Ho proposed " That this meeting of Golborneratspayers here- by request the Golborne Parochial Committee to urge the promoters of the new railway to bring tiler proposed line nearer this centre of the township than as now set forth in the company's plans ; and that if this is conceded the Com- mittee be requested to support the scheme." Mr John Garton seconded the motion, which was carried. The Chair- man signed the resolution, and undertook to hand it to the Parochial Committse. On the motion of Mr Benning- ton, it was suggested that the gradients be 1 in 80.—The Water Question: An important discussion ensued on the present charge, and also the quality supplied. The follow- ing resolution was subsequently pasEed : "That the Paro- chial Committee be requested to urge the Water Company to apply the most improved system of softsaing the town- ship water, and that the Committee be requested to consider at their earliest convenience the advisability of allowing consumers a discount off their water accounts." lie motion was carried nem con.—The Gas, Question: Mr Pen- nington said something should be said about the gas. The price was certainly excessive, and the quality was shame- ful. He proposed that the Parochial Committee agitate for an all-round, reduction in the price. As a proper remedy he advocated a local board who could either pnr- chase the gas works or erect one on their own account. The proposition respecting a reduction was adopted, but as there was a divided opinion respecting the economy of a local board no resolution was passed thereon.--A vote et Blanks to the Chairman .bnalzhi the meeth3K te it due.

TN PARLIAMENT.—SESSION 1885.—DISTRICT OF HAYDOCR, IN THE COUNTY OF LANCASTER. THE ST. HELENS AND WIGAN JUNCTIONS RAILWAY BILL, 1885. In pursuance of the provisions of the Act 35 and 36 Victoria, chapter 91, inlituled An Act to authorise the application of tunds of Municipal Corporations and other governing bodies in certain cases." Notice is Hereby Given. that a Special Met log of the Local Board for the district of Haydock, u the go- verning body of the said district, will be held in the Board- room, Haydock. on Wednesday, the 11th day of February next, at Three o'clock in the afternoon, for the following purposes, viz : To consider a Bill to be promoted in the next session of Parliament, called" The St. Helens and Wigan Junctions Railway Bill, 1885," and which Bill may be inspected at the office of the clerk to the said Board, Haydock. And for the purpose of considering, and, if deemed advisable, of passing the following resolution : Resolved, by an absolute majority of the whole number of the Local Board for the district of Haydock, and present at this meeting that in the judgment of the said Local Board assembled, being the governing body for the said district, it is expedient for such go- yarning body to oppose a Bill in Parliament to be promoted in the next session, called " The St. Helens and Wigan Junctions Railway Bill, 1885," and that the said Llcal Board, as such governing body of the said district do oppose the said Bill in Parliament, and f ,r that purpose apply the general district fund and general di trict rate under the con- trol of such governing body, or such portion V ereof as may benecessary for tt e payment of the costs and expenses attending the same. And Notice is Hereby further Given, that for the purposes aforesaid it is necessary that an absolute majority of the said Local Board should be present. Given under my band this 27th day of January, 1885. JOSEPH /VANS, Chairman of the said Local /bard.

James Wrigley and Son, Limited), BANEEES Manchester and Livelmool District Banking Co., Limited, Spring Gardens. Manchester, Water-street, Liverpool, 75, Comilla, London. Solicitors: Messrs. Ounliffe, Leaf, and Co., Manchester. Auditors : Messrs. Halliday, Pearson, and Co., Manchester. Secretary (pro tern) : Herbert Birch. Temporary Offices: 54, John Dalton-street, Manchester. Mr. H. M. Stan'ey, in his recent addresses, pointed out the advents ,es which must accrue to the manufacturing dis- tricts. of which Manchester is the centre, from the opening up of the new markets of the Congo Country in South West Africa. The decision of the Berlin Conference that absolute freedom ox trade shall be estab ished for a term of years on the Congo, will tend to develop trade with territories which have hitherto not been reached by commerce. Trade on the L)sver Congo has considerably increased dur- ing the last few years. Last year the imports into the Congo district amounted to £884,000, and the exports to about £1,858,400, so that in round figui es the trade may be placed at £2,800,000 per an • urn. This Company Is tormed to take advantage of a portiere of ibis actually-existing and increasing tradeaud to participite in the commercial development of these Congo markets. In order to avoid the manifest delays and obvious disadvan- tages and difficulties inseparable from an entirely new busi- ness, a provisional agreement has bean made with the Congo and Central African Company, Limited, of -Llverpaol, which possesses Faetorles and Stations at Ban tna, Emborna, St. Anto- nio. Chimposa Binda, Quissaage, L,assaia, Chichianga, and Chlmbica on the fiver Coago, and at Ambriz and Ambrizette on the Coast, where a small but profitable business has been carried on for the past two yea's. for the first of which (1883) over 10 per cent, woe earned for 1884 the accounts are not set completed, but the results are expec!ei to be of a similar character to the preceding year. By this Provisional Agreement, dated the 1203 day a Janu- ary, 1885, m tde between the Congo and Central African Com- pany, Limited, of the one part, and this Company of the other part, the Congo and Central African C,mprny, Limited. agrees to transfer its Stations, Factories, and Buildings, Stores, and Pant, Its Steamers, Cargo, Surf, and otter Boats to this Company from the Ist day of January, 1485. at a valuatisn. to te pad for by fully paid-up shares in this Company, and to sell its Stock of Goods, Merchandise, and Produce to this Company, at the cost price, as per inventories, made up to the 31st day of December, 1894. No payment will be made to the Congo and Central African Company, Limited, for Goodwill, the shareholders in that Company being satisfied that they will make a larger profit by becoming interested in a more powerf ully-coustituted under- taking. This agreement will provide the new Company at once with a favourable bask for Its operations, and enable it to enter Immediately upon a profitable businem in the Lower Congo District, under the direction and supervision of an efficient and reliable staff, and give great Iw:tittles for opening up trade as communications with the Upper Congo progress and are established. In alloting Shares the Directors will be guided by the prin- ciple of ratable distribution, but giving ame preference to order of application. Should no allotment be made, the amount paid on application will be returned in full. The Memorandum and Articles of Association can be in- spected at the Offices of the Company. Prospectus and Forms of Application for Shares can be ob- tained at the Offices of the Company, and from tile Bankers and Solicitors.
